lead: Today the Church honours St Joseph as the patron of workers, and our calendar also remembers Jeremiah the prophet. Both readings speak of ordinary work. Paul reminds the Thessalonians that he earned his own bread with his hands, and in the Gospel the people of Nazareth say of Jesus, “Is not this the carpenter’s son?” The Son of God spent most of his life in a workshop, and the town that knew him best could not believe that God had come so close. Jeremiah, who was rejected by the men of his own town, knew that sorrow too. The key words are work and offence.

r.h: We worked night and day
set: Paul founded the church in Thessalonica, the chief city of Macedonia, on his second missionary journey (Acts 17:1–9). Many scholars think that 2 Thessalonians was written by Paul soon after the first letter; others think a disciple wrote it in his name somewhat later. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way. The letter corrects those who were saying that “the day of the Lord is already here” (2:2), and many think this excitement had led some believers to stop working. Today's verses deal with them.
str: v. 6: keep away from those who live in idleness against the tradition received.
vv. 7–9: Paul's own example: he worked night and day so as to burden no one.
v. 10: the rule he gave when he was with them.
vv. 11–12: a command to the idle: work quietly and earn your own living.
kw: The word first meant a soldier out of rank, someone who breaks the line. Here it means a person who has left the ordinary order of daily duty. It is not about those who cannot work, but those who will not.
not doing any work, but busybodies
Paul makes a play on words in v. 11: not working but working around, busy with other people's affairs. The NRSV catches the sense with “mere busybodies”.
vv: but with toil and labor we worked night and day, so that we might not burden any of you.
Paul was a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3). He worked so that no one could say he preached the Gospel for money.
This was not because we do not have that right, but in order to give you an example to imitate.
An apostle had the right to be supported by the Church (1 Corinthians 9:14). Paul chose not to use it here, so that his life would teach as clearly as his words.
Anyone unwilling to work should not eat.

The word is “unwilling”, not “unable”. The sick, the old and the poor who cannot work are not the target of this verse. The early Church cared for them, as Paul's own collection for the poor shows (Romans 15:26).
ch: The Church sees in human work a share in God's own work of creation, and also a way of being united with Christ, who worked with his hands at Nazareth (CCC 2427). St John Paul II wrote a whole encyclical on work, Laborem Exercens (1981), where he teaches that work is for the person, and not the person for work. Pope Pius XII set the feast of St Joseph the Worker on 1 May in 1955, so that the day of workers would also be a day of prayer. Paul's words today are not harsh. They protect the community, and they protect the dignity of each person, who is made to give as well as to receive.

r.h: Is not this the carpenter’s son?
set: Matthew has just finished his great chapter of parables (13:1–52). Jesus now returns to Nazareth, his hometown. The people who watched him grow up hear his teaching and see his works, but they cannot get past what they already know about him. Mark tells the same story (Mark 6:1–6).
str: vv. 53–54a: Jesus teaches in the synagogue of his hometown.
vv. 54b–56: astonishment turns into questions about his family.
v. 57: they take offence; Jesus speaks of the prophet without honour.
v. 58: few deeds of power, because of their unbelief.
kw: A craftsman who worked with wood and sometimes stone: doors, ploughs, roof beams, houses. In Mark the people call Jesus himself “the carpenter” (Mark 6:3). Joseph taught his trade to the boy entrusted to him.
From skandalon, a stumbling block or a trap. Jesus was too ordinary for them. The very closeness of God became the stone they stumbled over.
vv: Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary?
The neighbours mean it as a put-down, but the reader of Matthew knows more. Joseph is “the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born” (1:16), and Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit (1:20).
And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?

In Hebrew and Aramaic the word for brother also covers cousins and close kin. Later Matthew names “Mary the mother of James and Joseph” among the women at the cross (27:56), a different Mary. The Church teaches that these are close relatives of Jesus, not other children of the Virgin Mary (CCC 500).
And he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.
Mark says Jesus “could do no deed of power there” (Mark 6:5). Matthew puts it more gently. The power of Jesus is never lacking; but he does not force himself on those who close their hearts.
ch: The Catechism reflects on the hidden life of Jesus at Nazareth: for most of his life he shared the condition of most people, a daily life of manual work, obedience to Mary and Joseph, and the religious life of his people (CCC 531–533). St John Paul II, in Redemptoris Custos (1989), and Pope Francis, in Patris Corde (2020), speak of Joseph as a working father who earned bread for the Holy Family and taught Jesus the value and dignity of work. Every honest work done with love can be offered to God.

qa: Did Jesus really have brothers and sisters?

The Gospels speak of the “brothers” of Jesus, but the word was used widely for relatives. James and Joseph are later said to be sons of another Mary (Matthew 27:56). The Church has always confessed that Mary remained a virgin, and understands these “brothers and sisters” as close relatives of Jesus (CCC 499–501).
rite: Our Syriac calendar keeps the memory of Jeremiah on this day. Jeremiah was a priest's son from Anathoth, a small town near Jerusalem, and the men of Anathoth threatened his life: “You shall not prophesy in the name of the Lord, or you will die by our hand” (Jeremiah 11:21). Today's Gospel is the same story in a new form: “Prophets are not without honor except in their own country.” St Joseph, the just and silent workman, and Jeremiah, the prophet who suffered for his message, together show us two faces of faithfulness: patient daily work and courage when the word of God is unwelcome.
study: How can my daily work, at home, in the field, the office or the kitchen, become an offering at the Holy Qurbono?
Is there someone close to me whom I find hard to take seriously because I know him or her too well?

lead: The Fifth Sunday after Qyomtho stands four days before the Ascension, and its readings speak of a joy that cannot be taken away. In the evening Gospel (John 16:12–15) Jesus promises: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth.” In 2 Samuel 5:9–12 David grows greater and greater, “for the Lord, the God of hosts, was with him.” Proverbs 10:1–13 teaches that “love covers all offenses”. Isaiah 28:23–29 watches a farmer at work and concludes that the Lord “is wonderful in counsel”. In Acts 13:44–52, even when Paul and Barnabas are driven out of Pisidian Antioch, “the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.”

We study three readings more closely. Deuteronomy 16 commands Israel to rejoice before the Lord at the festival of Weeks, the feast the Greek-speaking Jews called Pentecost. Colossians 3 tells the baptized that their life is now hidden with Christ, who is seated at the right hand of God. In John 16 Jesus tells his disciples that their pain will turn into joy, like the pain of a mother whose child is born. The key words are rejoice, above and a little while.

r.h: Rejoice before the Lord at the festival of weeks
set: Deuteronomy is given as Moses' great farewell speech on the plains of Moab, before Israel enters the land. Chapter 16 sets out the three pilgrim feasts, when every Israelite man was to appear before the Lord: the festival of unleavened bread, the festival of weeks and the festival of booths (16:16).

The festival of weeks came seven weeks after the beginning of the grain harvest (16:9). It was a harvest thanksgiving. Because it fell on the fiftieth day, Greek-speaking Jews called it Pentecost, “fiftieth”; the book of Tobit already speaks of “our festival of Pentecost, which is the sacred festival of weeks” (Tobit 2:1). Later Jewish tradition also linked this feast with the giving of the Law at Sinai.
str: v. 10: keep the festival with an offering in proportion to the blessing received.
v. 11: rejoice before the Lord, the whole household together with the Levite, the stranger, the orphan and the widow.
v. 12: remember that you were a slave in Egypt.
kw: Named after the seven weeks counted from the first sickle in the grain. The counting itself taught Israel that the whole harvest was a gift, measured out day by day from God's hand.
Deuteronomy commands joy again and again at the place God chooses (12:7, 12; 16:11, 14). Joy before God is not only a feeling; it is a duty of worship, and it is meant to be shared.
Memory is the root of Israel's mercy. Because they were once slaves, they must make room at the feast for those who have no land and no protector.
vv: Then you shall keep the festival of weeks to the Lord your God,
The feast belongs “to the Lord”. The harvest is his before it is ours.
you and your sons and your daughters, your male and female slaves, the Levites resident in your towns, as well as the strangers, the orphans, and the widows who are among you

The list is wide on purpose. No one is to be left outside the joy: not the servant, not the foreigner, not the child without a father, not the woman without a husband. A feast where the poor are missing is not yet the feast God wants.
Remember that you were a slave in Egypt, and diligently observe these statutes.
Gratitude for one's own rescue becomes kindness to others. The same reason is given for rest on the sabbath (5:15).
ch: The Church sees in this feast the background of the Christian Pentecost. The Holy Spirit came upon the disciples “when the day of Pentecost had come” (Acts 2:1), when Jews from every nation were gathered in Jerusalem for the festival. The Catechism teaches that on the day of Pentecost Christ's Passover is fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit (CCC 731). The harvest of the fields becomes the first harvest of the Church, when about three thousand were baptized (Acts 2:41). The command to share joy with the stranger, the orphan and the widow still stands: the early Church in Jerusalem shared its goods so that no one was in need (Acts 4:34).

r.h: Seek the things that are above
set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor, in modern Turkey. The church there was founded not by Paul but by his co-worker Epaphras (1:7). The letter speaks in Paul's name from prison. Many scholars think a disciple of Paul wrote it after his time, while others hold that Paul wrote it himself; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.

Chapter 2 warns against a “philosophy” of food rules, special days and the worship of angels (2:8, 16–18). Against all this the letter puts Baptism: “you were buried with him in baptism, you were also raised with him” (2:12). Today's verses draw the consequences for daily life.
str: vv. 1–4: you have been raised with Christ; seek what is above, for your life is hidden with him.
vv. 5–7: put to death what is earthly: impurity and greed, which is idolatry.
vv. 8–9a: put away anger, malice, slander and lies.
vv. 9b–11: you have put off the old self and put on the new, in which Christ is all and in all.
kw: seek the things that are above

“Above” is not a place in the sky. It is where Christ is, “seated at the right hand of God”, a phrase taken from Psalm 110:1. To seek what is above is to let the risen Christ set the direction of the whole life.
The tense means: has been hidden and stays hidden. The new life of the baptized is real now, but it cannot yet be seen. It will be revealed “when Christ who is your life is revealed”.

The new self is renewed “according to the image of its creator”, recalling Genesis 1:27. In 1:15 Christ himself is called “the image of the invisible God”. Baptism restores in us the likeness that sin had darkened.
vv: So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
The “if” does not express doubt. It means “since”. Because Baptism has joined us to the risen Lord, our desire must follow him.
for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
Hidden like seed in the earth, or like treasure kept safe. No one can steal what is kept “with Christ in God”.
Put to death, therefore, whatever in you is earthly: fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed (which is idolatry).
Greed is called idolatry because it puts money where God should be. Jesus said the same: “You cannot serve God and wealth” (Matthew 6:24).
In that renewal there is no longer Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave and free; but Christ is all and in all!
The Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were thought by Greeks to be the roughest of all peoples. In Christ the walls that divide human beings lose their power. Galatians 3:28 says the same.
ch: The Catechism uses these verses to teach that through Baptism Christians already share in a real way in the heavenly life of the risen Christ, though this life remains “hidden with Christ in God” (CCC 1003). The putting off of the old self and the putting on of the new was acted out in the early Church's baptisms, where the candidate took off old clothes, went down into the water and came up to be clothed in white. The Church still speaks of the white garment as a sign that the baptized have “put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27; CCC 1243). The list of sins in vv. 5–9 is a reminder that the new life is not only a gift to receive but a way of life to grow into, with the help of grace.

r.h: Your pain will turn into joy
set: John 13–17 is the farewell of Jesus at the Last Supper. He has told his disciples that he is going to the Father, and they are filled with sorrow (16:6). Just before today's reading he promised the Spirit of truth, who will guide them into all the truth (16:13), the evening Gospel of this Sunday.

In today's verses Jesus speaks of a short time of absence followed by a seeing again. The disciples do not understand. The reader knows the pattern: his death on Friday, his rising on the first day of the week, and then his going to the Father and his return at the end.
str: v. 16: a little while, and you will not see me; again a little while, and you will see me.
vv. 17–19: the disciples puzzle over “a little while”, and Jesus knows their question.
vv. 20–22: sorrow turned into joy, like a mother after childbirth.
vv. 23–24: on that day: ask the Father in my name, so that your joy may be complete.
kw: The phrase comes seven times in four verses (vv. 16–19). The disciples repeat it because it puzzles them. Christian readers have heard in it both the three days of the Passion and the whole time of the Church, which is short when set beside eternity.
The same word is used for the sorrow of the disciples and the pain of childbirth. Jesus does not deny their grief. He promises that it will be changed, not simply replaced.

The great word of the farewell discourse. Jesus wants “that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be complete” (15:11). This joy is rooted in seeing him again, and it is guarded by him, so “no one will take your joy from you”.
vv: A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me.

Two different Greek verbs stand behind “see” here. The second is the one Mary Magdalene uses on Easter morning: “I have seen the Lord” (20:18). The disciples will see the risen Lord, and through their witness the Church learns to see him with the eyes of faith.
you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.
Not pain followed by a different joy, but the pain itself becoming joy. The Cross that caused their grief becomes the source of their gladness.
When a woman is in labor, she has pain, because her hour has come.
The prophets used this image for Israel waiting for God's salvation (Isaiah 26:17; 66:7–9). “Her hour” recalls the hour of Jesus, which is the hour of his Passion and his glory (12:23; 13:1).
So you have pain now; but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.
Jesus does not only say “you will see me”, but “I will see you”. The initiative is his. A joy that depends on him cannot be taken away by others.
Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.
Prayer in the name of Jesus is new because the disciples now pray as those united to him. Its fruit is not only an answer to a request, but a joy that is full.
ch: St Augustine, preaching on this passage, took the second “little while” to mean the whole present age, which seems long to us but is short beside eternity (in substance). The Church lives in that “little while”, between the sorrow of the Cross and the full joy of seeing him face to face. The Catechism teaches that, after his Passover, Jesus taught his disciples to pray to the Father in his name, and that this is the newness of Christian prayer (CCC 2614–2615). The image of the woman in labour also helps Christians to understand suffering: not as meaningless, but as something God can turn toward new life (Romans 8:22–23).

qa: Can a Christian be commanded to rejoice when life is hard?

Deuteronomy commands joy, and Paul writes “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Philippians 4:4). This joy is not pretending that nothing hurts. Jesus himself says, “you will weep and mourn”. Christian joy rests on what God has done and promised, and so it can live alongside tears, as the disciples in Acts 13 were filled with joy even after they were driven out.
Does “if you ask anything of the Father in my name, he will give it to you” mean every prayer will be granted as I ask?

To pray in the name of Jesus is to pray as he prayed, in union with his will: “not what I want, but what you want” (Mark 14:36). The Father always gives what is good to those who ask (Matthew 7:11), and above all he gives the Holy Spirit (Luke 11:13). Sometimes the answer is not the thing asked for, but something greater.
Why do Christians read about a Jewish harvest feast?

Because the God who gave Israel the festival of weeks is the same God who poured out his Spirit on that feast in Jerusalem. The Church does not take this feast away from the Jewish people, who still keep it as Shavuot. She gives thanks that God's gifts to Israel are irrevocable (Romans 11:29; CCC 839), and she learns from Israel to rejoice before God and to remember the poor.
rite: In the Antiochene liturgy we pray, at the beginning of the Anaphora, that our minds and hearts may be lifted up on high, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God the Father. These words echo today's Epistle almost exactly. Every Holy Qurbono is a lesson in “seeking the things that are above”. This Sunday also leads us toward Suloko, the feast of the Ascension, on Thursday, and then to Pentecost. The Church of the Qyomtho season prays with the disciples for the Spirit, as Israel once counted the weeks toward the harvest feast.
study: Whom would Deuteronomy tell me to invite to my family's feasts this year?
Paul says that greed is idolatry. Where does money take the place of God in my life or in my home?
Jesus says that pain can be turned into joy. When have I seen this happen in my own life or in my family?
When the priest invites us in the Holy Qurbono to lift up our minds and hearts on high, what do I usually have on my mind?

lead: Today Paul cries out, “See, now is the acceptable time”, and describes an apostle's life as a string of paradoxes: sorrowful yet always rejoicing, having nothing yet possessing everything. In the Gospel Jesus says, “I am the light of the world.” The light of Christ shines most clearly in lives like Paul's, where human weakness and God's power meet. The key words are now and light.

r.h: Now is the acceptable time
set: Paul has just written that God “reconciled us to himself through Christ” and made him an ambassador with the message “be reconciled to God” (5:18–20). Now he urges the Corinthians not to let that grace go to waste, and he quotes Isaiah 49:8 in its Greek form. He then defends his ministry, not by listing successes, but by listing what he has suffered and how God has carried him through.
str: vv. 1–2: do not accept God's grace in vain; now is the day of salvation.
vv. 3–7: the servants of God commend themselves by endurance and by the gifts of the Spirit.
vv. 8–10: seven paradoxes of the apostolic life.
kw: Isaiah's Greek text had dektos, “acceptable”. Paul repeats the word with a stronger form, “most acceptable”. The time of God's favour that the prophet promised has arrived.
Paul says it twice: “now is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation”. The grace of God is never only for later. It meets us today.
vv: As we work together with him, we urge you also not to accept the grace of God in vain.
Paul calls himself a co-worker with God. Grace is pure gift, but it can be received “in vain” if it does not change the life of the one who receives it.
See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!
Paul adds his own comment to the prophet's words. He does not wait for a better moment to call his readers to conversion.
as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything.
These lines describe Christ himself, who “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor” (8:9). The apostle shares the pattern of his Lord.
ch: The Catechism quotes 2 Corinthians 6:2 when it speaks of the Last Judgement: the message of the Judgement calls people to conversion while God is still giving them “the acceptable time” and “the day of salvation” (CCC 1041). The Church has always seen in Paul's list of paradoxes a portrait of every faithful pastor and every Christian who suffers for Christ. What looks like loss is gain, because the life of Jesus is made visible in mortal flesh (4:10–11).

r.h: I am the light of the world
set: John sets these words at the festival of Booths (7:2). During that feast great lamps were lit in the Court of the Women in the Temple, and the light was said to shine over all Jerusalem. Jesus speaks “in the treasury of the temple” (8:20), which was in that same court. In the oldest manuscripts today's passage (8:12) follows directly on 7:52; the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is missing there and was placed here later, though the Church receives it as inspired Scripture.
The Pharisees object that a man cannot be a witness in his own case. Jesus answers that he is not alone: the Father bears witness with him.
str: v. 12: “I am the light of the world.”
vv. 13–18: the debate about valid testimony: Jesus and the Father as two witnesses.
vv. 19–20: “Where is your Father?”; his hour has not yet come.
kw: egō eimi to phōs tou kosmou
I am the light of the world

One of the great “I am” sayings in John. In the Old Testament light belongs to God: “The Lord is my light and my salvation” (Psalm 27:1). The Law too was called a lamp (Psalm 119:105). Jesus claims to be what the feast's lamps only pointed to.
A key word of John's Gospel. The Law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus' second witness is the Father, who speaks through his works and through the Scriptures (5:36–39).
vv: I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness but will have the light of life.
The promise is for those who “follow”, a word for discipleship. The pillar of fire led Israel through the desert at night (Exodus 13:21). Now the light walks ahead of us in person.
You judge by human standards; I judge no one.
Literally, “according to the flesh”, that is, by appearances. Jesus came not to condemn but to save (3:17).
You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also.
To know Jesus is to know the Father. Later Jesus says to Philip, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (14:9).
ch: The Church confesses Christ as “Light from Light” in the Creed. The Fathers called Baptism “enlightenment”, because those who receive it are filled with the light of the Word (CCC 1216). The Second Vatican Council begins its document on the Church with the words Lumen Gentium, “Christ is the light of the nations”, and adds that this light shines on the face of the Church (Lumen Gentium 1). The Church has no light of her own; she reflects his.

qa: Is Jesus attacking the Pharisees in this passage?

John shows a sharp debate, but Jesus is not rejecting the Pharisees as people. Many of them shared his faith in the resurrection and his love for the Law, and Nicodemus, a Pharisee, became a disciple (3:1; 19:39). The question at stake is who Jesus is, and it is put to every reader.
study: Paul says “now is the acceptable time”. What step toward God have I been putting off for later?
Where in my home or work do I most need the light of Christ to drive out darkness?

lead: Paul remembers how he first preached in Thessalonica: not with flattery or for gain, but gently, like a nurse caring for her children, sharing not only the Gospel but his own self. In the Gospel Jesus, insulted and accused of having a demon, answers with a promise: “Whoever keeps my word will never see death.” Both readings show the one who brings God's word paying the cost in person. The key words are gentle and keep.

r.h: Like a nurse tenderly caring for her own children
set: 1 Thessalonians is very probably the oldest book of the New Testament, written by Paul from Corinth around AD 50–51, only a few months after he had founded the church in Thessalonica. He had arrived there after being beaten and jailed in Philippi (Acts 16:22–24), and he had to leave Thessalonica in haste because of opposition (Acts 17:5–10). In this chapter he reminds the young church how he behaved among them, so that they would trust the Gospel he brought.
str: vv. 1–2: our coming was not in vain, though we came after suffering at Philippi.
vv. 3–6: not deceit, flattery or greed, but speech to please God.
vv. 7–8: gentle like a nurse; sharing our own selves.
vv. 9–12: work night and day; like a father urging his children to a life worthy of God.
kw: A woman who nurses and rears children, often a mother nursing her own. Paul, a man and an apostle, chooses a mother's image to describe his care. In v. 11 he adds a father's image too.

A real textual question in v. 7. Some ancient manuscripts read ēpioi, “gentle”, and others nēpioi, “infants”; the two Greek words differ by a single letter. The NRSV reads “gentle”, and notes the other reading. Either way, Paul says that he did not throw his weight about as an apostle.
vv: But we were gentle among you, like a nurse tenderly caring for her own children.
The tenderness of the apostle is not weakness. It is the way God himself cares for his people: “As a mother comforts her child, so I will comfort you” (Isaiah 66:13).
we are determined to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you have become very dear to us.
The Greek for “our own selves” is literally “our own souls”, that is, our lives. The Gospel is not passed on like a parcel. It is given with the life of the one who gives it.
urging and encouraging you and pleading that you lead a life worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.
The verb “calls” is in the present tense. God's call is not only a past event at Baptism; he keeps calling every day.
ch: The Church has always seen in this chapter a mirror for pastors, catechists and parents. Paul joins the images of mother and father, and every shepherd is asked to be both: tender in care and firm in guiding toward “a life worthy of God”. St Gregory the Great, in his Pastoral Rule, teaches that the one who governs souls must join gentleness with firmness, so that kindness does not become weakness and correction does not become harshness (in substance).

r.h: Whoever keeps my word will never see death
set: The debate in the Temple continues. In John, “the Jews” often means the Temple authorities and those who opposed Jesus in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus himself, his mother and all his first disciples were Jews. The insults in v. 48 show how hot the argument had become: “Samaritan” was a charge of being an outsider and a heretic, and “demon” a charge of madness.
str: v. 48: the insult: a Samaritan and possessed.
vv. 49–50: Jesus honours the Father and leaves judgement to him.
v. 51: the promise: whoever keeps my word will never see death.
kw: To keep a word is to guard it, hold on to it and live by it. The same verb is used for keeping commandments (14:15) and for the Father keeping the disciples safe (17:11).
A very strong negative in Greek: “will surely not see death”. Jesus does not deny that his disciples will die. He promises that death will not have the last word over them.
vv: I do not have a demon; but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me.
Jesus answers insult without insult. He refuses to defend his own honour and speaks only of the Father's.
Yet I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and he is the judge.
He leaves his cause in the Father's hands, as the suffering servant did: “he who vindicates me is near” (Isaiah 50:8).
Very truly, I tell you, whoever keeps my word will never see death.

His hearers take this literally and object that Abraham died (8:52). Jesus speaks of the life that begins now and does not end, as he says to Martha: “everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (11:26).
ch: The Catechism teaches that because of Christ, Christian death has a positive meaning: for those who die in Christ's grace, it is a share in his death so as to share in his Resurrection (CCC 1010). The Church also reads this hard debate with care. The Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in Christ's Passion cannot be blamed on all the Jews then living, nor on the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).

study: Paul shared “not only the gospel of God but also our own selves”. How do parents and catechists do this today?
When I am insulted, do I answer like Jesus, leaving my honour in the Father's hands?

lead: On the eve of Suloko, Paul asks the Thessalonians to pray for him, and assures them that “the Lord is faithful” and will guard them from the evil one. In the Gospel Jesus says that the eye is the lamp of the body: if the eye is healthy, the whole body is full of light. Prayer and a single-hearted gaze toward God prepare us to look up with the disciples tomorrow. The key words are faithful and healthy.

r.h: The Lord is faithful
set: These verses open the last part of the letter. Paul (or, as some scholars think, a disciple writing in his name) has finished correcting the false alarm about the day of the Lord. Now he asks for prayer, speaks of the opposition he faces, and entrusts the community to God before the practical warnings that follow (3:6–12, read on Saturday 1 May).
str: vv. 1–2: pray for us, that the word may spread and we may be rescued.
vv. 3–4: the Lord is faithful; we are confident in you.
v. 5: a blessing: may the Lord direct your hearts.
kw: Paul plays on words: “not all have faith (pistis). But the Lord is faithful (pistos).” Our faith may fail; God's faithfulness does not.
The Greek can mean “evil” or “the evil one”. The NRSV reads it as a person, as it does in the Lord's Prayer: “rescue us from the evil one” (Matthew 6:13).
vv: Finally, brothers and sisters, pray for us, so that the word of the Lord may spread rapidly and be glorified everywhere, just as it is among you,
Literally, “that the word of the Lord may run”. The great apostle does not think he can do without the prayers of a small young church.
But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one.
After speaking of his own dangers, Paul turns at once to theirs. His confidence is not in them, nor in himself, but in the Lord.
May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.
“The love of God” can mean both God's love for us and our love for God. “The steadfastness of Christ” is the patient endurance he showed, which he now shares with his own.
ch: The Catechism explains the last petition of the Our Father: the evil from which we ask to be delivered is not an abstraction but a person, Satan, the evil one, the angel who opposes God (CCC 2851). It also reminds us that we pray with confidence, because Christ has already conquered the evil one (CCC 2853). Paul's request for prayer is the root of the Church's constant custom of praying for her bishops, priests and missionaries.

r.h: Your eye is the lamp of your body
set: Luke places these sayings just after Jesus has refused to give a sign to “an evil generation”, except the sign of Jonah (11:29–32). The crowd wants proof, but the problem is not a lack of light. It is the eye that cannot see. Matthew has the same sayings in different places in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:15; 6:22–23).
str: v. 33: a lamp is put on a stand, not hidden.
v. 34: the eye is the lamp of the body: healthy or not healthy.
vv. 35–36: see that the light in you is not darkness; be full of light.
kw: Literally “single” or “simple”, undivided. It can also mean generous. An eye that is single looks at God without a double aim.
The same word that described the “evil generation” in v. 29. In Jewish speech an “evil eye” often meant a jealous or stingy eye (compare Matthew 20:15). The way we look at others shows what is in us.
vv: No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar, but on the lampstand so that those who enter may see the light.
The light of Jesus is not hidden. It is offered openly to all who come in.
Your eye is the lamp of your body. If your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light;
In the ancient world the eye was often thought of as a lamp that sends light out. Jesus uses the image to speak of the heart's way of seeing.
Therefore consider whether the light in you is not darkness.
A warning against self-deception. We can think we see while we are blind, as the Pharisees do in John 9:40–41.
ch: The Catechism links this teaching with purity of heart: the pure in heart are those who have attuned their minds and wills to God's holiness, and they are promised that they will see God (CCC 2518–2519; Matthew 5:8). A single eye is a heart that wants one thing, God, and so it sees others as God sees them.

study: For whom will I pray this week, as Paul asked the Thessalonians to pray for him?
Is my eye “single”? What double aims divide my way of looking at people?

lead: Suloko, the feast of the Ascension, gathers many readings around one movement: the Lord goes up, and his gifts come down. In the evening Gospel (Mark 16:14–20) the risen Lord says, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.” Deuteronomy 10:1–5 tells how Moses placed the new tablets of the covenant in the ark, and Jeremiah 31:31–34 promises a new covenant: “I will write it on their hearts.” In Isaiah 49:1–7 the servant is given “as a light to the nations”. In Acts 1:6–11 a cloud takes Jesus from the apostles' sight, and the angels say that “this Jesus” will come again “in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.”

We study three readings more closely. In 2 Kings 2 Elijah is taken up in a whirlwind, and Elisha, who sees him go, receives a double share of his spirit. In Ephesians 4 the Christ who ascended “far above all the heavens” gives gifts to his Church so that it may grow into his full stature. Luke ends his Gospel with Jesus lifting his hands in blessing and being carried up into heaven, while the disciples return to Jerusalem with great joy. The key words are taken up, gifts and blessing.

r.h: Elijah taken up; Elisha takes his mantle
set: Elijah, the great prophet of the ninth century BC, had stood alone for the Lord against the worship of Baal (1 Kings 18). His work was coming to an end, and he had been told to anoint Elisha as prophet in his place (1 Kings 19:16). Elisha had followed him ever since. At the start of chapter 2 we learn that “the Lord was about to take Elijah up to heaven by a whirlwind” (2:1), and Elisha refuses three times to leave his master's side.
Just before our verses Elijah strikes the Jordan with his mantle, the waters part, and the two cross on dry ground (2:8), as Israel once crossed the Jordan under Joshua (Joshua 3).
str: vv. 9–10: “Ask what I may do for you”: Elisha asks for a double share of Elijah's spirit, on condition that he sees him taken.
vv. 11–12: the chariot of fire; Elijah goes up in a whirlwind; Elisha cries out and tears his clothes.
vv. 13–14: Elisha takes up the mantle and parts the Jordan.
v. 15: the prophets of Jericho: “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.”
kw: The portion of the firstborn son, who received twice what the other sons received (Deuteronomy 21:17). Elisha does not ask to be greater than Elijah. He asks to be his heir, the son who carries on his father's work.
The prophet's cloak, the sign of his office. Elijah had thrown it over Elisha when he first called him from the plough (1 Kings 19:19). Now it falls to him for good.
A storm wind, the kind in which God speaks and acts (Job 38:1). Elijah does not die in the ordinary way; God takes him.
vv: Please let me inherit a double share of your spirit.
Elisha could have asked for anything. He asks for the one gift he needs to continue the mission. It is a model of prayer.
if you see me as I am being taken from you, it will be granted you; if not, it will not.
Seeing is the condition. The disciples too must be witnesses of the Lord's going up, “as they were watching” (Acts 1:9), before they receive the Spirit.
Father, father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!
Elisha calls Elijah his father and Israel's true defence, worth more than an army. The same words will be spoken over Elisha at his own death (13:14).
The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.
The master is gone, but his spirit remains in the disciple. The mission does not end when the prophet is taken up.
ch: The Fathers saw in Elijah's ascent a figure of Christ's Ascension, and also noted the difference. St Gregory the Great says that Elijah was taken up in a chariot, as one who needed help, while the Redeemer ascended by his own power (in substance). Elijah leaves his mantle and a double share of his spirit; Christ sends the Holy Spirit himself. Jesus tells his disciples to stay in the city “until you have been clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49), and in Acts 1:8 he promises, “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.” The Church is Elisha standing on the bank of the Jordan, holding the mantle and asking, “Where is the Lord?”, and finding that he is still at work.

r.h: He ascended and gave gifts
set: Ephesians is a letter about the Church as the body of Christ. It speaks in Paul's name, from prison (3:1; 4:1). Many scholars think it was written by a disciple of Paul after his death, while others hold that Paul wrote it; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.

Chapter 4 begins with a call to unity: “one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (4:4–5). Today's verses show that unity is not sameness. The one Lord gives different gifts to each, for the building up of the one body.
str: v. 7: grace is given to each according to the measure of Christ's gift.
vv. 8–10: a psalm explained: he ascended, and he who ascended first descended.
vv. 11–12: the gifts: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, to equip the saints.
vv. 13–16: growing up into Christ the head, speaking the truth in love.
kw: From Psalm 68:18, where God goes up to his holy mountain in triumph. The Hebrew says that he received gifts; Ephesians reads that he gave gifts, a reading also found in an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the psalm. The risen Christ does not take tribute; he gives.
A word used for setting a broken bone or mending nets (Mark 1:19). The ministers of the Church exist to make all the faithful fit for their own service.
Literally “truthing in love”: living and speaking the truth. Truth without love wounds; love without truth deceives. The body grows only when both are held together.
vv: But each of us was given grace according to the measure of Christ’s gift.
No one is left out. Every baptized person has received a gift for the good of the whole body.
He who descended is the same one who ascended far above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.
The Ascension is not Christ's absence from the world. He goes up in order to fill all things with his presence and his power.
to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ,
“The saints” are all the baptized. The pastors equip; all the faithful do the work of ministry, each in his or her place.
But speaking the truth in love, we must grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ,
The goal is maturity: not children tossed about by every wind of teaching, but grown men and women who reflect Christ.
ch: The Catechism quotes Ephesians 4:9–10 when it teaches that Christ descended into the realm of the dead before he ascended (CCC 631). Some interpreters read “the lower parts of the earth” as the Incarnation, his coming down to earth; others as his descent among the dead. Both readings agree that the one who went up is the one who first came all the way down. The Catechism also teaches that as Lord, Christ is head of the Church, which is his body, and that, taken up into heaven and glorified, he dwells on earth in his Church (CCC 668–669). The Second Vatican Council uses these verses to teach that the variety of ministries in the Church serves the unity of the one body (Lumen Gentium 7).

r.h: While he was blessing them, he was carried up into heaven
set: Luke tells the Ascension twice: here, at the end of his Gospel, and again at the start of Acts (Acts 1:6–11). Here it closes the long day of Easter that began at the empty tomb (24:1). Jesus has opened the Scriptures to the disciples and promised them “power from on high” (24:49). Now he leads them out to Bethany, on the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem.
str: v. 50: he leads them to Bethany and lifts his hands in blessing.
v. 51: while blessing them, he withdraws and is carried up into heaven.
vv. 52–53: they worship him, return with great joy, and bless God in the Temple.
kw: The verb comes three times in these four verses: Jesus blesses the disciples twice (vv. 50–51), and the disciples bless God (v. 53). The Gospel ends in an exchange of blessing between heaven and earth.
A passive verb: he was carried up, a way of saying that God the Father took him. The same verb is used in the Greek Old Testament for offerings carried up on the altar.
vv: Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them.

Luke's Gospel began with a priest, Zechariah, who came out of the sanctuary and could not speak the blessing (1:22). It ends with Jesus lifting his hands like the high priest Simon in Sirach 50:20, and blessing his people. The great High Priest completes what the old priesthood began.
While he was blessing them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.

He leaves while blessing. The last sight the disciples have of him is of hands raised over them. A few ancient manuscripts lack the words “and was carried up into heaven”, and also “they worshiped him” in v. 52; the NRSV, with most modern editions, keeps them, and they agree with Acts 1:9–11.
And they worshiped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy;
This is the first time in Luke's Gospel that the disciples worship Jesus. The angels' message at his birth was “good news of great joy” (2:10). The Gospel begins and ends in joy.
and they were continually in the temple blessing God.
Luke's Gospel began in the Temple (1:9) and ends there. The disciples wait in prayer, as Jesus told them, for the gift of the Spirit.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ's Ascension marks the definitive entrance of Jesus' humanity into God's heavenly domain, from where he will come again (CCC 665). Jesus Christ, the head of the Church, goes before us into the Father's glorious kingdom so that we, the members of his body, may live in the hope of one day being with him for ever (CCC 666). There, as the one priest of the new and eternal covenant, he intercedes for us without ceasing (CCC 662; Hebrews 7:25). The Ascension is not a sad parting. The disciples return “with great joy”, because the one who is gone from their sight is now with them in a new way, and their own humanity has gone ahead of them into heaven.

qa: Where did Jesus go? Is heaven up above the clouds?

Heaven is not a place in the sky, reached by travelling upward. The cloud in Acts 1:9 is the sign of God's presence, as it was at Sinai and at the Transfiguration. The Ascension means that the risen humanity of Jesus has entered fully into the glory of God, seated at the right hand of the Father (CCC 659–664). Scripture speaks of “going up” because that is how human beings naturally speak of what is above us in dignity.
If Jesus has gone up into heaven, how is he still with us?

He promised, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). He is present in his Church, in his word, in the poor, in prayer, and above all in the Holy Qurbono, where he is present truly, really and substantially (CCC 1373–1374). His Ascension is the beginning of a new nearness, through the Holy Spirit he sends.
Was Elijah's going up the same as Christ's Ascension?

No. Elijah was taken up by God, and Scripture does not say that he sits at God's right hand or that he sends the Spirit. Christ ascends as Lord and Son, in the humanity he took from the Virgin Mary, and he opens the way to heaven for all who are united to him (CCC 661). Elijah's story points ahead; Christ's fulfils it.
rite: Suloko is the Syriac word for “going up”. Our Church keeps the feast on Thursday, as the ancient Churches of both East and West have long done; our Latin neighbours in India keep it this year on the Sunday, 9 May. In the Syriac tradition we pray facing the east, the direction of the rising sun, waiting for the Lord who, the angels said, “will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). The days from Suloko to Pentecost are days of prayer with Mary and the apostles in the upper room (Acts 1:14), asking for the Spirit, as Elisha asked for a double share.
study: Elisha asked for one gift above all. If the Lord said to me, “Tell me what I may do for you”, what would I ask?
Ephesians says that every baptized person has received a gift. What is mine, and how am I using it for the body of Christ?
Jesus left his disciples while blessing them. Whom can I bless this week by word or deed?
How does the Ascension change the way I look at my own body, my work and my death?

lead: Our Church keeps today the feast of the Finding of the Cross, and it is also the First Friday of May. The Epistle gives us the last lines of Galatians, written in Paul's own hand: “May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The Gospel gives us the man who finds a treasure hidden in a field and the merchant who finds one pearl of great value, and both sell everything for what they have found. Paul is such a man. He found in the Cross the treasure for which he let everything else go. The key words are boast, treasure and new creation.

r.h: May I never boast of anything except the cross
set: Paul wrote to the churches of Galatia, in the interior of what is now Turkey, when some teachers were urging his Gentile converts to be circumcised and keep the Mosaic law in order to belong fully to God's people. The whole letter answers them: we are made right with God through faith in Christ, and the Spirit has been given to us.

Paul usually dictated his letters to a secretary and then added a few lines himself (compare 1 Corinthians 16:21; 2 Thessalonians 3:17). Here the secretary lays down the pen and Paul takes it up. In a few sentences he gathers the whole letter together: not the mark of circumcision, but the Cross; not the old order, but a new creation.
str: v. 11: Paul writes in his own hand, in large letters.
vv. 12–13: the motives of those who press circumcision on the Galatians.
v. 14: Paul's one boast: the cross of the Lord.
v. 15: what counts is a new creation.
v. 16: peace and mercy on those who keep this rule.
vv. 17–18: the marks of Jesus on his body; the closing blessing.
kw: To glory in something, to rest one's confidence and pride on it. Paul uses the word often. The opponents boast in the flesh of the circumcised (v. 13); Paul boasts in the Cross, the very thing the world thought shameful (1 Corinthians 1:23).
A measuring rod, a standard. From it comes the Church's word “canon”. The rule Paul gives is v. 15: what matters is not circumcision or uncircumcision, but the new creation God makes in Christ.

The brand that marked a slave or a soldier as belonging to his master. Paul means the scars of the beatings and stonings he suffered for Christ (2 Corinthians 11:23–25). They mark him as Christ's own.
vv: See what large letters I make when I am writing in my own hand!
Large letters were a way of underlining. Some have guessed that Paul's eyesight was poor (compare 4:15), but the plain point is emphasis: read this carefully.
May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
The Cross is not only something that happened to Jesus. It has changed Paul's relation to everything. The world's ways of ranking people, by race, rite or status, no longer have a hold on him.
For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything; but a new creation is everything!
Paul has said the same in 5:6: what counts is “faith working through love”. The new creation is what God does in the baptized (3:27).
peace be upon them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.

Scholars discuss whether “the Israel of God” means the whole Church of Jews and Gentiles in Christ, or the people of Israel, on whom Paul also prays God's mercy. Either way, Paul's blessing does not cancel God's love for Israel, as he will teach plainly in Romans 11:29.
for I carry the marks of Jesus branded on my body.

The opponents wanted a mark in the flesh. Paul has one already: the wounds of the Lord's servant. The Church later used the same word for the wounds of Christ seen in some saints, such as St Francis of Assisi.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Cross is the one sacrifice of Christ, the one mediator, and that he calls his disciples to take up their cross and follow him (CCC 618). It also teaches that Baptism makes the believer “a new creature”, an adopted child of God (CCC 1265). The Church's love for the Cross is not love of suffering for its own sake. It is love for the One who loved us and gave himself for us (2:20). The Roman liturgy opens the Mass of the Lord's Supper with words taken from verse 14, and the whole Church, East and West, sings of the Cross as the tree of life.

r.h: The treasure and the pearl
set: Chapter 13 is the third of the five great discourses in Matthew, the chapter of parables. Jesus first teaches the crowds from a boat; then he leaves them and goes into the house, where he explains the parables to his disciples (13:36). Today's parables are spoken to the disciples alone. The treasure, the pearl, the net and the master of the household are found only in Matthew.

In a land often crossed by armies, people sometimes buried their valuables in the ground, and some died without digging them up. A farm labourer might strike such a hoard with his plough. Pearls came from far away and were among the most costly things in the ancient world.
str: v. 44: the treasure hidden in a field.
vv. 45–46: the merchant and the one pearl.
vv. 47–48: the net that gathers every kind of fish.
vv. 49–50: the meaning of the net: the separation at the end of the age.
vv. 51–52: “Have you understood?”; the scribe who brings out what is new and what is old.
kw: The word of v. 44 returns in v. 52: the master of the household brings things “out of his treasure”. The disciple who has found the treasure of the Kingdom becomes himself a storehouse for others.
In the ancient world a single fine pearl could be worth a fortune. The merchant is a man who knows values. When he sees the one pearl, he knows that everything else he owns is worth less.
Literally, “discipled”. It is the same verb as the Lord's last command in Matthew: “make disciples of all nations” (28:19). A true scribe of the Kingdom is first of all a disciple.
vv: then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.
The word to notice is joy. He does not sell with regret, counting his losses. What he has found makes everything else easy to give up.
on finding one pearl of great value, he went and sold all that he had and bought it.
The first man stumbles on his treasure; the merchant has been searching. God's Kingdom is found both ways: by surprise, and by a long search.
a net that was thrown into the sea and caught fish of every kind;
The net does not choose while it is in the water. The Church gathers all kinds of people, and the sorting belongs to God at the end, not to us now.
brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old.
The new comes first. The disciple does not throw away the Law and the Prophets; he reads them in the light of Christ, who fulfils them (5:17).
ch: The Catechism uses these parables to show that the Kingdom asks for a radical choice: to gain it, one must give everything (CCC 546). St Irenaeus taught that the treasure hidden in the field is Christ, hidden in the Scriptures and revealed when they are opened (in substance). The Second Vatican Council quotes St Augustine's saying that the New Testament is hidden in the Old and the Old made plain in the New (Dei Verbum 16), which is the treasure of the scribe in v. 52. The Catechism quotes the same words, “the furnace of fire”, from the nearby parable of the weeds when it speaks of the reality of hell (CCC 1034), always as a call to conversion now.

qa: Was it honest for the man to hide the treasure and buy the field?

The parable does not ask us to judge his business ethics. Jesus often takes a story from ordinary life, even a doubtful one, to make one point (compare the dishonest manager in Luke 16:8). The point here is the joy that makes a person give everything for the Kingdom.
Was the Cross really found?

The tradition that St Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine, sought the Cross in Jerusalem around AD 326 is told by St Ambrose before the end of that century. Already about AD 350 St Cyril of Jerusalem told his catechumens that pieces of the wood of the Cross had spread through the whole world. The details of the story grew with time. The Church's feast does not rest on proving any one relic. It honours the Cross of the Lord, the sign of our salvation.
Does “the world has been crucified to me” mean that Christians must despise the world?

No. God made the world good and loves it (John 3:16). Paul means the world as a system of values that ranks people by status and flesh. That world has lost its hold on him. A Christian loves creation and people more, not less, when he no longer needs the world's approval.
rite: Our Church honours the holy Cross at many points of the year, above all on the feast of the Cross in September, and today on the feast of its finding. The Syriac tradition loves to call the Cross the tree of life, set again in the midst of the garden. In the Holy Qurbono the priest blesses the people with the hand cross, and we sign ourselves with it at the beginning and end of prayer. Today is also the First Friday, when many families come to Confession and the Holy Qurbono in honour of the Heart of Jesus, pierced on the Cross (John 19:34). The two belong together: the Cross is the treasure, and the pierced Heart shows why it was given.
study: What do I really boast in: my family name, my work, my achievements, or the Cross of the Lord?
The man sold everything “in his joy”. What would I find easy to give up if I truly saw the treasure of the Kingdom?
Paul carried the marks of Jesus on his body. What marks has faithfulness to Christ left on my life?
How can our family make the sign of the Cross with more attention and love this week?

lead: On the feast of Mar Yohannan Shleeha, St John the Apostle, both readings speak of love. Paul asks, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?”, and answers that nothing in all creation can. The Gospel shows the disciple whom Jesus loved, following the risen Lord, and tells us that his testimony is true. John's whole life was a following and a witnessing, held up by a love that did not let him go. The key words are love, follow and witness.

r.h: Nothing can separate us from the love of God
set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome, a church he had not founded, probably around AD 57 or 58, from Corinth, before taking the collection to Jerusalem (15:25–26). He hoped to visit Rome and go on to Spain. The letter sets out his gospel more fully than any other.

Chapter 8 describes life in the Spirit: no condemnation for those in Christ (8:1), the Spirit crying “Abba! Father!” in us (8:15), creation groaning in hope (8:22). From v. 31 Paul sings a hymn of confidence: “If God is for us, who is against us?” Today's verses are its climax.
str: v. 35: the question, and a list of hardships.
v. 36: a psalm of suffering (Psalm 44:22).
v. 37: in all these, more than conquerors.
vv. 38–39: no power in all creation can separate us from God's love in Christ.
kw: A word Paul seems to have coined: to win beyond winning. The victory is not that the hardships stop, but that they cannot break the bond with Christ. It comes “through him who loved us”.
Paul means Christ's love for us, not first our love for him. That is why nothing can separate us from it. Our love can grow weak; his does not.
A perfect tense: I have been persuaded and I remain so. Paul does not speak as one who hopes it may be true, but as one who has tested it in prisons, shipwrecks and beatings (2 Corinthians 11:23–27).
vv: Who will separate us from the love of Christ?
Paul's list is not imagined. He had known hardship, persecution, hunger, nakedness, danger and the threat of the sword. He names the worst and says they are not stronger than love.
As it is written, “For your sake we are being killed all day long; we are accounted as sheep to be slaughtered.”

Psalm 44 is the prayer of faithful people who suffer although they have not forsaken God. Paul does not hide that Christians may suffer in the same way. Suffering is not a sign that God has stopped loving.
No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
“In” all these things, not “after” them. The victory is given in the middle of trouble.
nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

The love of Christ in v. 35 is now called the love of God in Christ. For Paul they are one love. The only thing the list leaves out is our own deliberate refusal, and even that God's grace patiently seeks to overcome.
ch: The Church offers this passage among the readings for funerals, because it speaks the hope of Christians at the grave: not even death can separate us from God's love. The Catechism quotes the verse that comes just before, “all things work together for good for those who love God” (8:28), when it teaches that God can bring good out of evil (CCC 313). The martyrs of every age, the Apostle John among the witnesses who suffered for Christ, have shown that this is not a fine phrase but a lived truth.

r.h: The disciple whom Jesus loved
set: Chapter 21 is the epilogue of John's Gospel. By the Sea of Tiberias the risen Lord has given the disciples a great catch of fish and shared a meal of bread and fish with them. Then he has asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?”, entrusted his sheep to him, and foretold the death by which Peter would glorify God (21:15–19). He ends with the command, “Follow me.”

Now Peter turns and sees another disciple. The Gospel never gives his name. It calls him “the disciple whom Jesus loved”, the one who reclined next to Jesus at the supper (13:23), stood by the Cross with the Mother of Jesus (19:26–27) and ran with Peter to the tomb (20:2–8). From the second century the Church has identified him with John the son of Zebedee.
str: v. 20: Peter sees the beloved disciple following.
v. 21: “Lord, what about him?”
v. 22: Jesus' answer: what is that to you? Follow me!
v. 23: a rumour corrected.
v. 24: this disciple is the witness who wrote these things.
kw: The word of discipleship from the first chapter, when two disciples followed Jesus and asked where he was staying (1:37–38). The beloved disciple is already following before Peter is told to.

One of John's favourite words, often translated “abide”: “Abide in me as I abide in you” (15:4). Here it means to remain alive until the Lord comes, but the Johannine reader hears more: this disciple's life was one long abiding.
John's Gospel is full of witnesses: John the Baptist, the Samaritan woman, the works of Jesus, the Father, the Spirit. It ends by naming its own author as a witness whose testimony is true.
vv: Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them;
He does not need to be called. Love has already made him a follower.
Lord, what about him?
Peter has just heard that he will die for Christ. It is natural to ask about another's path. Jesus will not compare.
what is that to you? Follow me!
Each disciple has his own road. Peter will shepherd and die on a cross; John will live long and bear witness. Both follow the same Lord.
This is the disciple who is testifying to these things and has written them, and we know that his testimony is true.
The “we” is the community around the disciple, who vouch for his word. The Gospel rests on an eyewitness who loved and was loved.
ch: St Irenaeus, writing around AD 180, says that John, the disciple of the Lord who leaned on his breast, published his Gospel while living at Ephesus (in substance). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the four Gospels are of apostolic origin and faithfully hand on what Jesus really did and taught (Dei Verbum 18–19). St Jerome tells that the aged John, carried into the assembly at Ephesus, would only say, “Little children, love one another”, and when asked why, answered that this is the Lord's command, and if it alone is kept, it is enough (in substance).

qa: Is the beloved disciple certainly John the son of Zebedee?

The Gospel itself does not name him, and scholars have discussed the question at length. From St Irenaeus onward the tradition of the Church has identified him with the Apostle John, and the liturgy honours John as the Evangelist. What is certain from the text is that the Gospel rests on the witness of a disciple who was close to Jesus at the supper, at the Cross and at the empty tomb.
Did the rumour mean that John would never die?

No, and the Gospel corrects it at once: Jesus did not say he would not die. According to early tradition John lived to a great age at Ephesus and died there. He was the witness who remained, while Peter was the shepherd who gave his life.
Was there rivalry between Peter and John?

The Gospel shows them together, not as rivals: at the supper, at the tomb, at the lake. Peter receives from Christ the charge to feed the sheep; John is the witness who first recognises the Lord (21:7). The Church needs both the shepherd's authority, which comes from Christ, and the beloved disciple's contemplation.
rite: Our Church honours Mar Yohannan Shleeha today, as the Byzantine Churches also do on this day; the Latin Church keeps his main feast on 27 December. The beloved disciple took the Mother of Jesus into his own home (John 19:27), and every Christian family is invited to do the same. He leaned on the Lord's breast at the supper, and in the Holy Qurbono we come to the same table and receive the same Lord. As we receive the Holy Mysteries this Saturday, we ask Mar Yohannan to teach us to follow without comparing, and to love as we have been loved.
study: Peter asked, “What about him?” When do I compare my path with someone else's instead of following?
Paul's list of hardships ends in confidence. Which hardship in my life most tempts me to doubt God's love?
The beloved disciple took Mary into his home. How does our family make room for the Mother of the Lord?
If Jesus' one command were “love one another”, as John repeated in old age, what would change in our home this week?

lead: The Sixth Sunday after Qyomtho falls between Suloko, the Ascension, which our Church kept on Thursday, and Pentecost next Sunday. All the readings speak of a Lord who goes away and yet does not leave his people alone. In the evening Gospel (John 17:1–5) Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven: “Father, the hour has come.” In Exodus 6:1–8 God tells Moses his name and promises to set his people at liberty. Wisdom 12:1–11 praises God's immortal spirit in all things and his patience, correcting sinners little by little. In Isaiah 44:21–28 God has swept away his people's sins like a cloud and calls them to return. In Acts 1:12–14 the apostles return from the Mount of Olives and devote themselves to prayer with Mary, the mother of Jesus.

We study three readings more closely. In Joshua 1:5–9 Moses has died, and God promises his successor: “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you.” Paul prays that the eyes of our hearts may be enlightened to see the power that raised Christ and seated him at the right hand of the Father. In John 16 Jesus tells his sad disciples that it is to their advantage that he goes away, because then the Advocate will come. The key words are with you, enlightened and Advocate.

r.h: As I was with Moses, so I will be with you
set: The book of Deuteronomy ends with the death of Moses on Mount Nebo, in sight of the promised land which he would not enter (Deuteronomy 34). The book of Joshua opens at that moment of loss: “My servant Moses is dead” (1:2). The people stand on the east bank of the Jordan. Their great leader is gone, and the land before them is not yet theirs.

Joshua had been Moses' assistant from his youth (Numbers 11:28) and was appointed his successor with the laying on of hands (Numbers 27:18–23; Deuteronomy 34:9). Many scholars think the book of Joshua took its final form much later, as part of a long history running from Deuteronomy to Kings, written to call Israel to faithfulness.
str: v. 5: the promise of God's presence: as with Moses, so with you.
v. 6: be strong and courageous: you will lead the people into the land.
vv. 7–8: the law of Moses: do not turn aside; meditate on it day and night.
v. 9: the command repeated: do not fear, for the Lord is with you.
kw: The words come three times in these few verses (vv. 6, 7, 9), and Moses had said them to Joshua before (Deuteronomy 31:7). The courage asked of Joshua does not come from his own strength but from the promise that God is with him.

The word means to murmur, to speak in a low voice. In the ancient world people read aloud, even alone. To meditate on the law day and night is to keep repeating God's word until it fills the mind, as in Psalm 1:2.
The name means “the Lord saves”. In Greek it is written Iēsous, the same as the name of Jesus. Moses had changed his name from Hoshea to Joshua (Numbers 13:16).
vv: As I was with Moses, so I will be with you; I will not fail you or forsake you.
The leader changes; the Lord does not. The letter to the Hebrews takes up this promise for all believers: “I will never leave you or forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).
do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left,
The way of God is pictured as a road. One can fall off on either side, by too little or by too much. Faithfulness walks straight on.
you shall meditate on it day and night,
Joshua is a soldier and a leader, yet his first task is to keep God's word in his mouth. Action without the word becomes blind.
do not be frightened or dismayed, for the Lord your God is with you wherever you go.
The promise ends with the same truth with which it began. Fear is not answered by an argument but by a presence.
ch: The Fathers saw in Joshua a figure of Jesus. St Justin Martyr points out that the one who led the people into the land bore the same name as Jesus, who leads us into our true inheritance (in substance), and Origen preached a whole series of homilies on Joshua in this light. The Catechism explains that the name Jesus means “God saves” (CCC 430). The Church also reads Joshua's story at this season for its pattern of departure and presence: Moses goes, and the Lord remains with his people; Jesus ascends, and the Spirit comes. What God said to Joshua, the risen Lord says to his Church: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

r.h: With the eyes of your heart enlightened
set: Ephesians presents itself as a letter of Paul written from prison (3:1; 4:1). Many scholars think it was written after his lifetime by a disciple who gathered up his teaching, while others hold that Paul wrote it himself; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way. It may have been meant for several churches of the province of Asia, since some early manuscripts lack the words “in Ephesus” in 1:1.

The letter opens with a long hymn of blessing (1:3–14) for all that God has done in Christ. In today's verses the hymn turns into a prayer. Paul thanks God for the faith and love of his readers and asks that they may see what they have been given. The prayer ends where this season is: with Christ raised and seated at the right hand of the Father.
str: vv. 15–16: thanksgiving for the readers' faith and love.
v. 17: prayer for a spirit of wisdom and revelation.
vv. 18–19: that they may know three things: the hope, the inheritance, the power.
vv. 20–21: that power at work in raising and enthroning Christ.
vv. 22–23: Christ, head over all things for the Church, his body.
kw: For the Bible the heart is the centre of the person, the place of thought and decision, not only of feeling. Paul prays for an inner sight, a seeing with the whole self, which only God can give.
Christ is head both over all things and of the Church. As head he rules, and as head he gives life to the body, as the head does to its members (4:15–16).

The Church is called “the fullness of him who fills all in all”. The phrase is difficult; it may mean that the Church is filled by Christ, or that in some way she completes him as a body completes its head. Either way, the Church is not an organisation beside Christ but his body, filled with his life.
vv: may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation as you come to know him,
Paul does not pray first that they may do more, but that they may know God better. The Christian life grows from knowing him.
so that, with the eyes of your heart enlightened, you may know what is the hope to which he has called you,
In the early Church Baptism was often called enlightenment (compare Hebrews 6:4). The baptized have received a new light, and Paul prays that it may grow.
God put this power to work in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places,
The same power is “for us who believe” (v. 19). The power that raised Christ is at work in his people.
has made him the head over all things for the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.
The Ascension does not take Christ away from the Church. He reigns over all things for the sake of his body.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ's sitting at the right hand of the Father means the beginning of the reign of the Messiah (CCC 663–664), and that Christ, raised and exalted, is the head of the Church, which is his body (CCC 669; 792). The Second Vatican Council develops the image of the Church as Christ's body, in which he pours out his life on the believers through the sacraments (Lumen Gentium 7). The prayer of these verses is a good prayer for every parish between the Ascension and Pentecost: that we may see the hope, the inheritance and the power we have been given.

r.h: It is to your advantage that I go away
set: Jesus speaks these words at the Last Supper, in the long farewell discourse of John 13–17. He has washed his disciples' feet, given them the new commandment, and warned them that the world will hate them as it hated him (15:18–25). Now he tells them plainly that he is going, and they are filled with sorrow.

In this discourse Jesus speaks five times of the Holy Spirit as the Paraclete, the Advocate (14:16–17; 14:26; 15:26; 16:7–11; 16:13–15). Today's passage is the fourth. It shows the Spirit not only as the comforter of the disciples but as the one who brings the truth about Jesus before the world.
str: vv. 5–6: Jesus is going to the Father; the disciples' sorrow.
v. 7: it is to your advantage: the Advocate will come.
v. 8: he will prove the world wrong about sin, righteousness and judgment.
vv. 9–11: the three explained: unbelief, Jesus' going to the Father, the condemnation of the ruler of this world.
kw: One called to stand beside another, especially in a court: a defender, helper, counsellor. Jesus has been their Paraclete; now he promises “another Advocate” (14:16).

The same verb Caiaphas used when he said that it was better for one man to die for the people (11:50). Caiaphas spoke more truly than he knew. The death and departure of Jesus are for the good of all.

A word from the law court: to bring out the truth, to show someone their error so that they may see it. The Spirit will reopen the trial of Jesus, in which the world thought it judged him, and show where the truth lay.
vv: yet none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’
Peter and Thomas had asked something like this earlier (13:36; 14:5). Now the disciples are too filled with sorrow to ask. Their grief looks only at what they are losing, not at where he is going.
it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you;
The Spirit is the fruit of the whole Paschal mystery. Only when Jesus has been glorified will the Spirit be given (7:39). His going is not loss but gift.
And when he comes, he will prove the world wrong about sin and righteousness and judgment:
Three words from a trial. The world judged Jesus a sinner, condemned him, and thought itself righteous. The Spirit reverses that verdict.
about judgment, because the ruler of this world has been condemned.
At the Cross it is not Jesus who is condemned, but the power of evil. Jesus had said, “now the ruler of this world will be driven out” (12:31).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Spirit, the other Paraclete, is promised when the hour of Jesus' glorification has come, and that he will prove the world wrong about sin, righteousness and judgment (CCC 729). It explains that conversion begins when the Spirit convinces us of sin, and at the same time gives the grace of repentance (CCC 1433). St John Paul II's encyclical on the Holy Spirit, Dominum et Vivificantem (1986), gives a long reflection on these verses, teaching that the Spirit convinces of sin in order to save, never to crush. The Spirit's work is like a doctor's: he shows the wound so that it can be healed.

qa: How can Jesus' going away be good for us?

While Jesus walked in Galilee he could be in one place at a time. Glorified at the right hand of the Father, he sends the Spirit, who makes him present to every believer, in every place, above all in the sacraments. The Catechism says the Spirit makes present the mystery of Christ (CCC 1092). We do not have less of Christ since the Ascension, but more.
Does “the world” here mean that everyone outside the Church is condemned?

No. In John, “the world” can mean the creation God loves (3:16) or the human order that closes itself against God. The Spirit convicts the world in order to bring it to truth and life. It is the ruler of this world who is condemned, not the people God wants to save.
Why do some Catholics in India keep the Ascension today?

The Ascension falls on a Thursday, and our Church kept Suloko on that day. In the Latin Church the bishops of a country may, with the approval of the Holy See, move the feast to the following Sunday so that more people can take part. The Latin Church in India does so, and keeps it today. The mystery is the same; only the day differs.
rite: The days between Suloko and Pentecost are days of prayer with Mary and the apostles in the upper room, as today's reading from Acts shows. In every Holy Qurbono the priest calls down the Holy Spirit on the offerings and on the people, and the whole Church becomes, in a small way, the upper room waiting for the Spirit. Our Latin brothers and sisters in India celebrate the Ascension today. Next Sunday our Church keeps Pentecost, the fiftieth day. This week is a good time for families to pray each day for the gifts of the Spirit, so that the eyes of our hearts may be enlightened.
study: Joshua had to lead without Moses. When have I had to go on without someone I relied on, and how was God with me?
Paul prays for “the eyes of your heart”. What do I need God to help me see this week?
Jesus says his going away is to our advantage. How is the Holy Spirit's presence in the sacraments a gift greater than seeing Jesus with our eyes?
The apostles prayed with Mary before Pentecost. How can our family keep these days with her?

lead: On the feast of Mar Shemun Shleeha, St Simon the Apostle, called the Zealot, the readings show two kinds of zeal turned toward Christ. In the Epistle Paul plans his journeys with zeal for the Gospel: a wide door has opened in Ephesus, and he will stay there until Pentecost. In the Gospel a rich tax collector, eager to see Jesus, runs ahead and climbs a tree, and the Lord invites himself into his house. Simon's zeal, whatever it was before, became zeal for the Lord who came “to seek out and to save the lost”. The key words are door, today and seek.

r.h: A wide door for effective work has opened
set: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, as verse 8 shows, probably around AD 53 to 55. He had founded the church in Corinth some years before (Acts 18:1–11). The letter answers many questions and troubles: divisions, a case of incest, lawsuits, marriage, food offered to idols, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts, the resurrection.

Chapter 16 is the practical close of the letter: the collection for the poor of Jerusalem, travel plans, news of fellow workers, and greetings. Even these plain lines show how the apostles worked: as a team, under God's providence, with care for one another.
str: vv. 5–7: Paul will come after passing through Macedonia, and hopes to stay some time.
vv. 8–9: he will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost: a wide door, many adversaries.
vv. 10–11: receive Timothy well and send him back in peace.
v. 12: Apollos will come when he has the opportunity.
kw: The fiftieth day, the Jewish Feast of Weeks, counted seven weeks from the offering of the first sheaf (Leviticus 23:15–16; Deuteronomy 16:9–10). Paul still reckons his year by Israel's feasts. For Christians the same day had become the day of the Spirit (Acts 2:1).
