Paul often speaks of an open door for the Gospel (2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3), and Luke uses the same image of the door of faith opened to the Gentiles (Acts 14:27). The door is opened by God; the apostle's task is to go through it.
Work that is active and bears fruit. The open door does not mean an easy road. In the same verse Paul says that “there are many adversaries”.
vv: if the Lord permits.
Paul makes plans, and good ones, but always under God's will. James gives the same counsel: “If the Lord wishes, we will live and do this or that” (James 4:15).
But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost,
These few words fix the place of writing and show that Paul kept the rhythm of the Jewish year.
for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.
Opportunity and opposition come together. Acts tells of the riot of the silversmiths in Ephesus, who feared that Paul's preaching would ruin the trade in images of Artemis (Acts 19:23–41).
for he is doing the work of the Lord just as I am;
Timothy was young (1 Timothy 4:12) and perhaps timid. Paul asks the Corinthians to respect him as they would the apostle himself, because the work is the Lord's.
He will come when he has the opportunity.
Some in Corinth had set Apollos against Paul (1:12; 3:4–6). Paul speaks of him warmly as “our brother”. The apostles did not compete.
ch: The Church sees in these lines that mission is the work of many, sent and supported by a community. The Catechism teaches that on the day of Pentecost, when the seven weeks of Easter had come to an end, Christ's Passover was fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit (CCC 731). Paul's waiting in Ephesus “until Pentecost” fits this season well: the Church in these days waits and prays, and then goes through the doors God opens. Paul's respect for Timothy and Apollos also teaches the Church's ministers to support one another rather than compete.

r.h: Today salvation has come to this house
set: This is Jesus' last stop before he goes up to Jerusalem. Luke has told the long journey since 9:51, and just before this, near Jericho, Jesus has healed a blind beggar who cried out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (18:35–43). The story of Zacchaeus is found only in Luke.

Jericho, near the Jordan, was a rich city on an important road, a natural place for collecting taxes and tolls. Tax collectors worked for the Roman authorities through contractors, and many grew rich by charging more than was due. They were despised by their neighbours as collaborators and cheats.
str: vv. 1–4: Zacchaeus wants to see Jesus and climbs a sycamore tree.
vv. 5–6: Jesus calls him by name and comes to his house; Zacchaeus welcomes him with joy.
v. 7: the crowd grumbles.
v. 8: Zacchaeus gives half to the poor and promises fourfold restitution.
vv. 9–10: salvation today; the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost.
kw: A word found nowhere else in the New Testament. Zacchaeus was not just a tax collector but the head of others, and rich. Luke has just said how hard it is for the rich to enter the Kingdom (18:24–27); here is a rich man who enters.

A key word of Luke's Gospel: “to you is born this day a Saviour” (2:11), “Today this scripture has been fulfilled” (4:21), “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43). Salvation is not only for later. It comes today.
Zacchaeus “was trying to see” (literally, was seeking to see) who Jesus was (v. 3). At the end we learn that the Son of Man came to seek the lost (v. 10). The man who sought was himself being sought.
vv: He was trying to see who Jesus was,
Perhaps curiosity, perhaps something deeper. God can use even a small desire to begin a great conversion.
Zacchaeus, hurry and come down; for I must stay at your house today.
Jesus calls him by name before Zacchaeus has said anything. The word “must” is the language of God's plan in Luke: this visit is part of the Saviour's mission.
Look, half of my possessions, Lord, I will give to the poor;

The law required one who stole a sheep to repay four sheep (Exodus 22:1). Zacchaeus goes beyond what anyone would demand. Some scholars, noting that the Greek verbs are in the present tense, read his words as a description of what he already did; many others see a conversion here, the fruit of Jesus' welcome.
Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.
The man the crowd had written off is restored to the people of God. Salvation comes to “this house”: conversion touches a whole household.
For the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost.
The words recall Ezekiel 34, where God promises to seek out his lost sheep himself. In Jesus the Shepherd has come.
ch: The Catechism uses Zacchaeus to teach that justice requires restitution of what has been taken wrongly: “if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I will pay back four times as much” (CCC 2412). It also notes that Jesus' welcome of sinners at table expresses in an astonishing way God's forgiveness and their return to the people of God (CCC 1443). The order matters: Jesus first comes to Zacchaeus' house, and then Zacchaeus changes. Grace comes first, and conversion is our answer to it.

qa: Who was Simon the Zealot?

He is one of the Twelve, named in every list of the apostles. Luke calls him “the Zealot” (Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13); Mark and Matthew call him “the Cananaean” (Mark 3:18; Matthew 10:4), from an Aramaic word that also means zealous, not from the land of Canaan. It may mean that he had belonged to a group zealous for the Law and for Israel's freedom, or simply that he was a man of great zeal. Later traditions about where he preached differ, and we cannot be sure of them.
Was it a sin to be a tax collector?

The work itself was not forbidden. When tax collectors asked John the Baptist what to do, he did not tell them to leave their work but to collect no more than was due (Luke 3:12–13). The sin was the fraud and greed that often went with it. Zacchaeus' conversion shows itself in honesty and generosity.
Why did the crowd grumble?

They saw Jesus going to the house of a man everyone knew as a sinner, and they thought it made Jesus unclean or approved the man's ways. Luke shows the same grumbling when Jesus eats with sinners (15:2). Jesus' answer is always the same: he came for the lost.
rite: Our Church honours Mar Shemun Shleeha today, as the Byzantine Churches also do; the Latin Church keeps his feast with St Jude on 28 October. Shleeha means one who is sent. We know little of Simon's life, but we know the most important thing: Jesus chose him, and his zeal was turned into zeal for the Kingdom. In the Holy Qurbono the Lord comes to our house as he came to the house of Zacchaeus, and Holy Communion is meant to bear fruit in honesty, generosity and the making good of wrongs. We ask Mar Shemun to pray that our zeal may always be the zeal of love.
study: What “door” has God opened for me to share the faith, and what “adversaries” make me hesitate?
Zacchaeus climbed a tree to see Jesus. What effort am I willing to make to see him more clearly?
Is there anything I have taken wrongly, in money, time or reputation, that I need to give back?
Simon was called the Zealot. What am I zealous about, and how can that zeal serve Christ?

lead: On the memory of Sts Cyril and Methodius, apostles of the Slav peoples, the Epistle praises God's plan to gather up all things in Christ, and the Gospel shows Jesus praying all night before he chooses the Twelve. God's plan reaches every people through those whom Christ sends. The key words are gather up, seal and apostles.

r.h: To gather up all things in Christ
set: In the Greek, Ephesians 1:3–14 is one long sentence of blessing, praising the Father who chose us, the Son in whom we are redeemed, and the Spirit with whom we are sealed. Today's verses are its second half. On Sunday we heard the prayer that follows this hymn (1:15–23).
str: vv. 7–10: redemption and forgiveness; the mystery of God's will: to gather up all things in Christ.
vv. 11–12: we who first hoped in Christ have an inheritance.
vv. 13–14: you also, hearing and believing, were sealed with the Spirit, the pledge of our inheritance.
kw: Literally, to sum up under one head (kephalē). All things, in heaven and on earth, scattered by sin, are to be brought together in Christ. St Irenaeus built his teaching of “recapitulation” on this word.
A seal marked ownership and protected what was sealed. The baptized are marked as God's own by the Holy Spirit.
A down payment, the first part of a price that guarantees the rest. The Spirit is God's first gift and the promise of all that is to come.
vv: In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses,
Redemption is the language of setting slaves at liberty. It is paid, Paul says, not in silver but in the blood of Christ.
to gather up all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.
God's plan is not to save a few souls out of a ruined world, but to bring the whole creation into unity in Christ.
were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit;
Hearing, believing, being sealed: the path of every Christian, from the word preached to the sacraments received.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Confirmation, like Baptism, marks the Christian with an indelible seal, the sign that he belongs totally to Christ, and it cites this passage (CCC 1295–1296). St Irenaeus taught that Christ “recapitulated” in himself the whole history of humanity, undoing Adam's disobedience by his obedience (in substance). Cyril and Methodius gave the Slav peoples the Scriptures and the liturgy in their own tongue, so that they too could hear “the word of truth” and be gathered into Christ.

r.h: He spent the night in prayer and chose the Twelve
set: Opposition to Jesus is growing. After he healed a man's withered hand on the sabbath, his opponents “were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus” (6:11). At this moment Jesus goes up the mountain to pray. Luke shows Jesus praying before every great moment: at his baptism (3:21), before Peter's confession (9:18), at the Transfiguration (9:28–29) and on the Mount of Olives (22:41).
str: v. 12: a night of prayer on the mountain.
v. 13: at daybreak he chooses twelve and names them apostles.
vv. 14–16: the names, from Simon Peter to Judas Iscariot.
kw: A word used only here in the New Testament. The choice of the Twelve is born of a whole night with the Father.
One who is sent, an envoy. Twelve recalls the twelve tribes of Israel: Jesus is gathering and renewing God's people.
vv: he spent the night in prayer to God.
Before he acts, Jesus prays. The Church still prays before choosing her ministers, as she did before the choice of Matthias (Acts 1:24).
chose twelve of them, whom he also named apostles:
From a larger group of disciples Jesus chooses some for a special mission. Today's saints, Cyril and Methodius, are called “apostles of the Slavs” because they continued that mission.
and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
Luke does not hide it. Judas too was chosen after a night of prayer. God's call is real, and so is human freedom.
ch: The Catechism notes that Jesus prays before the decisive moments of his mission, including the choice of the Twelve (CCC 2600). It teaches that Jesus chose the Twelve with Peter as their head and that they are the foundation stones of the Church (CCC 765), and that the apostles' mission continues in the bishops, their successors (CCC 860–862).

qa: Why did Jesus choose Judas, if he knew he would betray him?

The Gospels do not answer every question. They show that Jesus' choice was real and his love sincere, and that Judas chose to turn away. Even the betrayal could not defeat God's plan; God brought salvation out of it.
rite: Sts Cyril and Methodius were brothers from Thessalonica in the ninth century. They went as missionaries to the Slav peoples of Moravia, created an alphabet for their language, and translated the Scriptures and the liturgy into Slavonic. Pope Adrian II approved their Slavonic liturgy in Rome. St John Paul II named them co-patrons of Europe (1980) and wrote of them in the encyclical Slavorum Apostoli (1985). The Byzantine Churches honour them today, and the Latin Church on 14 February. Our own Church knows the gift they gave: we pray the Holy Qurbono of the ancient Antiochene tradition in Malayalam, while keeping the treasures of Syriac.
study: Paul says the Spirit is the pledge of our inheritance. How do I live as one who has already received God's first gift?
Jesus prayed all night before an important choice. What decision in my life should I bring to prayer before I act?

lead: Paul tells the Philippians to work out their salvation, because it is God who is at work in them, and to shine like stars in a crooked world. In the Gospel Jesus asks the crowds why they can read the sky but not the present time, and urges them to settle with their accuser while they are still on the way. Both readings say: now is the time to respond to God. The key words are work out, shine and the present time.

r.h: God is at work in you
set: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison (1:13), to a church he loved and that had supported him. Today's verses follow the great hymn to Christ, who emptied himself, became obedient to death on a cross, and was exalted by God (2:6–11). Paul's “Therefore” draws the lesson: let the mind of Christ shape your life.
str: vv. 12–13: work out your salvation, for God is at work in you.
vv. 14–16: without grumbling, shine like stars, holding fast to the word of life.
vv. 17–18: Paul poured out as a libation; joy shared.
kw: To bring to completion. Salvation is God's gift, and the believer must let it work through his whole life. The same root appears in v. 13 for God's own working.
God's activity within us. He gives both the will and the doing. Our effort is not in competition with grace; it is grace bearing fruit in us.
I am poured out as a libation
A drink offering of wine poured over a sacrifice. Paul sees his possible death as an offering poured out over the faith of the Philippians (compare 2 Timothy 4:6).
vv: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling;
Fear and trembling here is not terror but reverent seriousness before God, the attitude of one who knows that something holy has been entrusted to him.
for it is God who is at work in you, enabling you both to will and to work for his good pleasure.
The reason for our effort is God's prior action. We work because God is working, not to make him begin.
in which you shine like stars in the world.
The words recall Moses' song about a “crooked and perverse generation” (Deuteronomy 32:5), and Daniel's promise that the wise will shine like the stars (Daniel 12:3).
ch: The Catechism teaches that justification establishes cooperation between God's grace and human freedom (CCC 1993). St Augustine said that God, who created us without us, did not will to save us without us (quoted in CCC 1847). Verse 13 guards against the opposite error: everything good in us, even the wish to do good, is from God's grace. Works done in grace are truly ours and truly his.

r.h: Interpret the present time
set: Jesus is on his long journey to Jerusalem (9:51). He has just spoken of the fire he came to bring and of the division his coming will cause, even within families (12:49–53). Now he turns to the crowds. In the land of Israel, clouds from the west come off the Mediterranean and bring rain; the south wind comes from the desert and brings heat. People knew these signs well.
str: vv. 54–56: you can read the weather; why not the present time?
v. 57: judge for yourselves what is right.
vv. 58–59: settle with your accuser on the way, before it is too late.
kw: Originally a stage actor, one who wears a mask. Jesus means people who are clever about one thing and pretend not to see another.
Not clock time but the decisive moment, the time of opportunity. In Jesus, God's time has come, and it calls for a response.
The smallest coin in use, worth a tiny fraction of a day's wage. It is the coin of the poor widow (21:2).
vv: You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?
The signs of God's visit were before them: the sick healed, the poor hearing good news (7:22). They could read clouds, but not this.
And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?
Jesus appeals to conscience. One does not need to wait for others to tell us that it is time to change.
on the way make an effort to settle the case,
Like a debtor on the road to court, we are on the way to God's judgment. Now, while we are still on the way, is the time to be reconciled.
ch: Matthew places a similar saying in the Sermon on the Mount, as a call to be reconciled with a brother (Matthew 5:25–26). The Church reads Luke's version above all as a call to conversion while there is time. Some Fathers also saw in the “last penny” a picture of the purification after death (in substance), but the Church's teaching on purgatory rests on the whole of Tradition and Scripture, not on this verse alone (CCC 1030–1032).

rite: Our Syriac calendar remembers two bishops of the fourth century today. Mar Epiphanios was born in Palestine and became bishop of Salamis in Cyprus; he wrote against the heresies of his time and died in AD 403. Mar Yaqob, bishop of Nisibis, took part in the Council of Nicaea in AD 325 and died in 338; tradition counts Mar Aprem among his disciples. Both shone like stars in difficult times and held fast to the word of life.
study: Paul says God is at work in me. Where do I most need to trust his working rather than only my own effort?
With whom do I need to be reconciled “on the way”, before it is too late?

lead: Three days before Pentecost both readings speak of what God has promised and how surely he keeps it. Hebrews calls our hope “a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul”, fixed where Jesus has gone before us. In John, Jesus stands up at the feast of Booths and promises rivers of living water, and the evangelist explains: “he said this about the Spirit.” Today the Church also remembers Mar Ishaq of Antioch, a teacher and poet of the Syriac Church. The key words are anchor and living water.

r.h: Hope, a sure and steadfast anchor
set: Hebrews is a sermon in written form for Christians who were growing weary. Just before this passage the author warns against falling away and then encourages his readers: God is not unjust, he will not forget your love (6:10). To show that the promise is certain he goes back to Abraham, to whom God swore an oath after the near sacrifice of Isaac (Genesis 22:16–17).
str: vv. 13–15: God's oath to Abraham, and Abraham's patience.
vv. 16–18: why an oath: two unchangeable things, the promise and the oath.
vv. 19–20: hope as an anchor, reaching behind the curtain, where Jesus has entered.
kw: In the ancient world the anchor was a picture of steadiness and hope. Early Christians carved it on tombs in the Roman catacombs, sometimes shaped like a cross. Here the anchor is not dropped into the sea below but cast upward, into heaven.

A runner sent ahead, or a scout who goes first so that others can follow. Jesus has not entered heaven only for himself. He has gone ahead “on our behalf”, and where he is, his people are meant to come.
vv: When God made a promise to Abraham, because he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself,
The words of Genesis 22:16 are “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord.” God binds himself with his own name.
We have this hope, a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters the inner shrine behind the curtain,
The curtain is the veil before the Holy of Holies in the tabernacle, where the high priest entered only once a year (Leviticus 16). Our hope reaches into the very presence of God.
where Jesus, a forerunner on our behalf, has entered, having become a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.
This verse leads into chapter 7, where Melchizedek, the priest-king who brought out bread and wine (Genesis 14:18), becomes a figure of the eternal priesthood of Christ.
ch: The Church reads this passage as a lesson in Christian hope. The Catechism calls hope the virtue by which we desire the Kingdom of heaven and eternal life, placing our trust in Christ's promises and relying on the grace of the Holy Spirit, and it quotes this very verse about the anchor (CCC 1817, 1820). Hope is not a guess about the future. It rests on God's word, and God does not go back on his word.

r.h: Let anyone who is thirsty come to me
set: The scene is the feast of Booths (Tabernacles), the autumn harvest feast in Jerusalem (John 7:2). Later Jewish sources (the Mishnah, tractate Sukkah) describe how on each day of the feast water was drawn from the pool of Siloam and poured out at the altar, with prayer for the rains. Many scholars think this rite stands behind Jesus' cry on “the great day”. The feast also recalled the water from the rock in the wilderness (Exodus 17; Numbers 20).
str: vv. 37–38: Jesus' cry: come, drink; rivers of living water.
v. 39: the evangelist's comment: this is the Spirit, not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified.
kw: In everyday Greek and Hebrew, “living water” is fresh running water from a spring, not water kept in a cistern. Jesus used the same words to the Samaritan woman (4:10). Here John says plainly what it means: the Holy Spirit.

In John, Jesus is “glorified” in his hour: his Cross, Resurrection and return to the Father (12:23; 17:1). The Spirit is given from the glorified Christ. On the Cross water flows from his side (19:34); on Easter evening he breathes the Spirit on the disciples (20:22).
vv: Let anyone who is thirsty come to me,
Jesus stands and cries out, as a teacher who wants everyone to hear. The invitation echoes Isaiah 55:1: “Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters.”
Out of the believer’s heart shall flow rivers of living water.

The Greek is literally “out of his belly”. Ancient punctuation can be read two ways: the rivers flow from the believer, or from Christ, if we read “let the one who believes in me drink” together with v. 37. Many Fathers took it of Christ, the rock from whom the water flows; both readings are found, and both are true in their own way. No single verse of the Old Testament says these exact words; John seems to gather passages such as Ezekiel 47:1–12 and Zechariah 14:8.
for as yet there was no Spirit, because Jesus was not yet glorified.
This does not mean the Spirit did not exist. Some manuscripts add “given”, and that is the sense: the Spirit had not yet been poured out as the gift of the risen Lord.
ch: The Church hears in this Gospel the promise of Pentecost and of Baptism. The Catechism names water among the symbols of the Holy Spirit and links it to the water from Christ's pierced side (CCC 694). Every baptized Christian has drunk of this water. The same Spirit wants to flow out through us to others, so that our homes and parishes become springs and not stagnant pools.

qa: Who was Mar Ishaq of Antioch?

He was a Syriac teacher and poet, usually placed in the fifth century, and many metrical homilies (memre) have come down under his name. Scholars think that the writings under the name Isaac may come from more than one author of that time. Our Church honours him as a Malpan, a teacher of the faith in song.
study: What anchors my soul when life is stormy: God's promise, or something smaller?
Where do I feel thirsty in my spiritual life, and how can I come to Jesus to drink before Pentecost?

lead: Today the Church remembers Mar Addai, whom the Syriac tradition honours as the apostle of Edessa. Both readings suit a missionary. Paul writes from prison that he has learned to be content in plenty and in want, because “I can do all things through him who strengthens me.” In Luke, Jesus tells his friends that what is whispered will be proclaimed from the housetops, and that they need not fear, for God counts even the hairs of their heads. The key words are contentment and do not fear.

r.h: I have learned to be content
set: Paul writes to the church at Philippi, the first church he founded in Europe (Acts 16), while he is a prisoner (1:13). The place is disputed: Rome is the traditional answer, and some scholars suggest Ephesus or Caesarea. The Philippians had sent him a gift by the hand of Epaphroditus (4:18). Near the end of the letter Paul thanks them warmly, but in a careful way: he is grateful, yet he does not want them to think he depends on gifts more than on Christ.
str: v. 10: joy at the Philippians' renewed care.
vv. 11–12: Paul has learned contentment in every condition.
v. 13: the source of his strength: Christ.
v. 14: thanks for sharing his distress.
kw: The Stoic philosophers used this word for a person who needs nothing outside himself. Paul takes the word and changes its meaning. He is not self-sufficient but Christ-sufficient: his contentment comes from “him who strengthens me”.

Literally “I have been initiated”, a word connected with the mystery cults of the Greek world. Paul uses it with a touch of irony: the great “secret” he has been let into is how to be hungry and full alike in Christ.
From koinōnia, fellowship. The Philippians did not only send money. They made Paul's suffering their own (1:5, 7).
vv: for I have learned to be content with whatever I have.
Contentment is learned, not born. Even Paul had to learn it, step by step, through hardship.
I know what it is to have little, and I know what it is to have plenty.
Paul knew both. Too much can be as great a test as too little, and he had learned to stay steady in both.
I can do all things through him who strengthens me.
This is not a promise that we can achieve anything we like. In context it means: in every situation, in hunger or in plenty, Christ gives the strength to stay faithful.
ch: The Church reads this passage as a lesson in Christian poverty of spirit and trust. The Catechism teaches that the Lord grieves over the rich who find consolation in abundance, and calls all to detachment from riches so as to enter the Kingdom (CCC 2544–2547). Paul shows the other side: gratitude for gifts received, and a heart that is not ruled by them. Missionaries like Mar Addai lived this way.

r.h: Do not be afraid
set: Jesus is on the long journey to Jerusalem that fills the middle of Luke's Gospel (9:51–19:27). Just before this passage he has sharply criticized some Pharisees and lawyers at a meal (11:37–54). Now, with thousands crowding around, he speaks first to his disciples. Luke presents a warning about hypocrisy followed by an encouragement to fearless witness.
str: v. 1: beware of the yeast of hypocrisy.
vv. 2–3: what is hidden will be revealed.
vv. 4–5: whom to fear and whom not to fear.
vv. 6–7: the sparrows and the hairs of the head: God's care.
kw: A little yeast spreads through the whole dough (Galatians 5:9). Here it stands for a hidden influence that slowly corrupts. Jesus names it: hypocrisy.
The Greek word for an actor's part on the stage. A hypocrite wears a mask: he shows one face in public and hides another.
Gehenna, the valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, once a place of terrible idolatry (Jeremiah 7:31). In Jewish teaching of the time it had become a name for the place of final punishment.
vv: I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that can do nothing more.
Only here in the Synoptic Gospels does Jesus call the disciples “my friends”. The friends of Jesus will face persecution, but they are not left alone.
fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell.
This is God, not the devil. The fear of God is not terror before a tyrant, but the reverence that puts everything else in its place. Whoever fears God need fear no one else.
Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten in God’s sight.
In Matthew 10:29 two sparrows are sold for a penny; here five for two pennies, as if the fifth were thrown in for nothing. Even that one is not forgotten.
ch: The Church hears in this Gospel the call to sincere and courageous witness. The Catechism teaches that the disciple must not only keep the faith and live on it, but also profess it, bear witness to it with assurance and spread it (CCC 1816). In many lands Christians still suffer for their faith. We pray for them and for those who wrong them, and we trust the word of Jesus: “Do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.”

qa: Who was Mar Addai?

The Syriac tradition remembers Addai as one of the seventy (or seventy-two) disciples of the Lord, sent after the Ascension to Edessa, where King Abgar welcomed the Gospel. The story is told in the ancient Syriac Teaching of Addai, and Eusebius of Caesarea gives an earlier form of it, where the missionary is called Thaddeus (Church History 1.13). Historians debate the details, but the story shows how early the faith took root among the Syriac-speaking peoples.
rite: Our Church prays in the Syriac tradition, and Edessa was one of its great early centres. The Anaphora of the Apostles Addai and Mari is still used by the East Syriac Churches, including our sister Church, the Syro-Malabar Church. Honouring Mar Addai, we thank God for the missionaries who first carried the Gospel in the language that shaped our liturgy.
study: Paul learned to be content in plenty and in want. Which of the two is harder for me, and why?
Is there a part of my life where I wear a mask? What would it mean to let God's light into it?

lead: Today the Syriac calendar remembers the Holy Mother of God for the ears of grain, asking her prayers over the ripening harvest, and also St Pachomius, father of monks who live in community. The readings fit the day beautifully. Paul speaks of sowing and reaping, of a God “who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food”. In Luke a woman blesses the mother of Jesus, and Jesus answers that those who hear the word of God and obey it are blessed. Mary is blessed in both ways. The key words are sowing and hearing.

r.h: God loves a cheerful giver
set: Chapters 8 and 9 of 2 Corinthians are about the collection Paul was gathering among his Gentile churches for the poor Christians of Jerusalem (see also Romans 15:25–27; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4). For Paul this gift was more than charity. It was a sign of the unity between the Gentile churches and the mother church from which the Gospel had come to them. Many scholars think chapters 8 and 9 may once have been separate notes, but they belong together in theme.
str: v. 6: the rule of the harvest: sparingly or bountifully.
v. 7: give willingly and cheerfully.
vv. 8–10: God's power to provide, with Psalm 112 and an echo of Isaiah 55.
kw: From this word comes the English “hilarious”. Paul's phrase recalls the Greek Old Testament of Proverbs 22:8, which has a line not in the Hebrew: “God blesses a cheerful and generous man.” The point is not noise but gladness: giving that comes from joy, not pressure.
Literally “with blessings”. The same word, eulogia, is used in 9:5 for the gift itself. A gift given generously is a blessing for the one who gives and the one who receives.
vv: the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
A farmer who keeps back his seed out of fear will have a poor harvest. Generosity is a kind of trust in God.
for God loves a cheerful giver.
God looks at the heart of the giver more than at the size of the gift, as Jesus saw in the widow's two coins (Mark 12:41–44).
He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing
These words echo Isaiah 55:10, where the rain gives “seed to the sower and bread to the eater”, a picture of God's word that does not return empty.
ch: The Church reads this passage when she speaks of almsgiving and the sharing of goods. The Catechism teaches that giving alms to the poor is a witness to fraternal charity and a work of justice pleasing to God (CCC 2462), and it lists the corporal works of mercy (CCC 2447). On a day when the Church prays over the harvest, Paul reminds us that every harvest is God's gift, given to be shared.

r.h: Blessed are those who hear the word of God
set: Jesus has just answered those who said he cast out demons by Beelzebul (11:14–26). A woman in the crowd, moved by his words, cries out a blessing on his mother. This short scene is found only in Luke. It recalls Elizabeth's blessing in 1:42–45 and Mary's own words, “all generations will call me blessed” (1:48).
str: v. 27: a woman blesses the mother of Jesus.
v. 28: Jesus' answer: blessed are those who hear and keep the word of God.
kw: The word of the Beatitudes (6:20–22). It speaks of the happiness that comes from God, not of good luck.

A small Greek word with a large meaning. It can mean “no, rather” or “yes, but even more”. Here Jesus does not deny the woman's praise; he widens it and goes deeper: what makes a person truly blessed is hearing and keeping the word.
The verb means to guard or keep watch over something precious. Luke twice says that Mary “treasured” all these things in her heart (2:19, 51).
vv: Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you!
A common way in that world of praising a son by praising his mother. Without knowing it, the woman fulfils Mary's prophecy that all generations would call her blessed.
Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it!

Jesus does not set Mary aside. He names the deeper reason for her blessedness. She is the first to hear the word and keep it: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word” (1:38).
ch: The Second Vatican Council cites this passage when it speaks of Mary during her Son's public ministry: he declared blessed those who hear and keep the word of God, as she was faithfully doing (Lumen Gentium 58). St Augustine taught that Mary was more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ (On Holy Virginity 3, in substance). Mary's motherhood and her faith are not rivals. She conceived the Word in her heart before she conceived him in her womb.

qa: Is Jesus correcting the woman, or lowering his mother?

No. The word he uses can mean “yes, but even more”. Elsewhere Luke shows Mary as the model of one who hears the word and keeps it (1:38, 45; 2:19, 51; 8:21). Jesus' answer is the highest praise of his mother, and it opens her blessedness to every disciple who listens as she did.
rite: The Syriac tradition keeps three commemorations of the Mother of God tied to the farming year: for the seeds in January, for the ears of grain in May, and for the vines in August. In Kerala, where life still follows the rains and the harvest, these days teach that Mary prays for our daily bread as well as for our souls. Today is also the memory of Mar Pachomios (Pachomius), the Egyptian monk of the fourth century who first gathered monks into a common life under a written rule. Our monks and religious owe much to him.
study: Am I a sparing sower or a bountiful one, with my time, my money and my kindness?
How can I, like Mary, hear the word of God this week and keep it in my heart?

lead: On the Sunday of Pentecost every reading speaks of the Spirit of God coming to rest on his people. In the evening Gospel (John 14:25–31) Jesus promises that “the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything”. In Numbers 11:16–35 the Lord takes some of the spirit that was on Moses and puts it on the seventy elders, and Moses cries, “Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets, and that the Lord would put his spirit on them!” Joshua 18:1–7 shows the whole congregation gathered at Shiloh around the tent of meeting, where each tribe receives its share by lot and the Levites receive the priesthood as their heritage. In 1 Samuel 10:9–16 the spirit of God comes upon Saul and he is changed, so that people ask, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”

We study four readings more closely, because on this feast the Acts of the Apostles cannot be passed over. Ezekiel promises a new heart and a new spirit. Acts tells how the promise was fulfilled on the day of Pentecost in Jerusalem. Paul teaches that the one Spirit gives many gifts, to each for the common good. In John, Jesus promises another Advocate and says that the Father and he will come and make their home with those who love him. The key words are spirit, gift and home.

r.h: A new heart and a new spirit
set: Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon with the first group of exiles in 597 BC. He prophesied there before and after the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC. Chapters 1–24 announce the judgment; after the news of the city's fall (33:21), the book turns to hope. Chapter 36 promises that the people will return to their land, and chapter 37 follows with the vision of the dry bones that live again when the breath of God enters them.

The starting point is surprising. God does not act because Israel has earned it, but “for the sake of my holy name”. In the ancient world a defeated people seemed to prove that its god was weak. The exile had made the nations think little of the Lord. God will now show who he is by renewing his people from within.
str: vv. 22–23: not for your sake, but for my holy name.
vv. 24–28: gathering, cleansing, a new heart, my spirit within you, my people and your God.
vv. 29–30: abundance of grain and fruit.
vv. 31–32: remembrance and shame that lead to repentance.
vv. 33–38: rebuilt towns, a land like Eden, and cities full of people like the flocks at the festivals.
¶ The centre of the passage is vv. 26–27: the gift of a new heart and of God's own spirit.
kw: In Hebrew thought the heart is not only the seat of feeling but the centre of thought, will and decision. A new heart means a new person, able at last to choose what God wills.

The same word means wind, breath and spirit. In v. 26 God gives “a new spirit”; in v. 27 he goes further: “my spirit”. In the next chapter the rûaḥ blows over the valley of dry bones and they live (37:9–10).
heart of stone, heart of flesh
A heart of stone is hard, cold and unable to respond. A heart of flesh is living and tender. The phrase is not about weakness but about life.
vv: It is not for your sake, O house of Israel, that I am about to act, but for the sake of my holy name,
Salvation begins with God's faithfulness to himself, not with our merits. That is good news: what depends on God cannot fail.
I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses,
The sprinkling recalls the purification rites of the Law (Numbers 19). Christians have always heard Baptism in these words.
A new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you; and I will remove from your body the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.
Jeremiah had promised a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Ezekiel adds how it will happen: by the gift of the spirit.
you shall be my people, and I will be your God.
The covenant formula, the heart of the whole Old Testament. The new heart is given so that the covenant may at last be lived.
ch: The Catechism names Ezekiel 36 among the prophetic oracles that directly concern the sending of the Holy Spirit, in which God speaks to the heart of his people in the language of promise (CCC 715). The Church sees the promise fulfilled at Pentecost and in every Baptism, when water and the Spirit make a person new. The first beneficiaries of the promise were the people of Israel, and the Church never forgets that God's gifts to them are irrevocable (Romans 11:29; CCC 839).

r.h: When the day of Pentecost had come
set: Pentecost, Greek for “fiftieth”, is the Jewish feast of Weeks (Shavuot), kept fifty days after Passover at the end of the grain harvest (Leviticus 23:15–21; Deuteronomy 16:9–12). It was one of the three pilgrim feasts, so Jerusalem was full of Jews from many lands. Later Jewish tradition linked this feast with the giving of the Law at Sinai, and some scholars think the link was already known in the time of the apostles.

Luke has prepared this moment. The risen Lord told the disciples to wait in the city for “the promise of the Father” (Acts 1:4), and the apostles devoted themselves to prayer, “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (1:14).
str: v. 1: the day and the gathering.
vv. 2–4: wind, fire and the gift of the Spirit; they speak in other languages.
vv. 5–11: devout Jews from every nation hear in their own languages.
vv. 12–13: two reactions: wonder and mockery.
¶ Peter's sermon follows (2:14–41), explaining the event from the prophet Joel.
kw: Pnoē, breath or blast of wind, is close to pneuma, spirit. As at creation (Genesis 2:7) and in Ezekiel's valley (Ezekiel 37), the breath of God gives life.

Fire is a sign of God's presence: the burning bush, the pillar of fire, the fire on Sinai (Exodus 3:2; 13:21; 19:18). John the Baptist had said that the Messiah would baptize “with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke 3:16).
The word in vv. 6 and 8 means the speech of a people or region. Luke stresses that each heard in his own tongue. The Gospel does not erase languages and cultures; it speaks in all of them.
vv: When the day of Pentecost had come, they were all together in one place.
Literally “when the day was being fulfilled”. The feast reaches its true meaning. The disciples are together, in unity and prayer, when the gift comes.
Divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them.
One fire, divided among many, resting on each. The Spirit is given to the whole community and to every person in it.
All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit gave them ability.
Luke means real languages that the hearers understood, as vv. 6–11 show. This differs from the gift of tongues Paul discusses in 1 Corinthians 14, which needed an interpreter.
in our own languages we hear them speaking about God’s deeds of power.
The list of nations runs from Parthia in the east to Rome in the west. The first thing the Spirit does is to make the Church speak of God's great works.
ch: The Catechism teaches that on the day of Pentecost, when the seven weeks of Easter had come to an end, Christ's Passover is fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, who is manifested, given and communicated as a divine person (CCC 731). Many Fathers saw here Babel undone: where pride had scattered the nations in confusion of speech (Genesis 11:9), the Spirit gathers them in one faith, each in his own language (for example St Augustine, in substance). The Church is catholic from her first day.

r.h: Varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit
set: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, around AD 54–55 (16:8). The church at Corinth was gifted but divided: rival parties, disorder at the Lord's Supper, and pride over spiritual gifts, especially speaking in tongues. Chapters 12–14 deal with these gifts. Chapter 12 gives the principle, chapter 13 the more excellent way of love, and chapter 14 practical order in worship.
str: vv. 1–3: the test of the Spirit: “Jesus is Lord”.
vv. 4–6: one Spirit, one Lord, one God in many gifts, services and activities.
v. 7: each gift is for the common good.
vv. 8–10: a list of gifts.
v. 11: one Spirit gives to each as he chooses.
kw: The word in v. 1 can mean “spiritual things” or “spiritual people”. The Corinthians may have used it proudly of themselves. Paul quickly turns to another word, charismata.
From charis, grace. A charism is a gift of grace, not a prize for holiness. It is given, never earned.
Literally “for what is profitable”. Gifts are not trophies for display; they are tools for building up the body. Paul develops this with the picture of the body in vv. 12–27.
vv: no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit.
“Jesus is Lord” is perhaps the oldest Christian creed. To say it truly, with the heart, is already a sign of the Spirit at work.
Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit;
Verses 4–6 name the Spirit, the Lord and God. The Church has long seen in this the pattern of the Holy Trinity: one God acting in many ways.
To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
“To each”: no baptized person is without a gift. “For the common good”: no gift is only for oneself.
All these are activated by one and the same Spirit, who allots to each one individually just as the Spirit chooses.
The Spirit is not a force we control but a person who chooses. Gifts are received with gratitude, not demanded.
ch: The Catechism opens its teaching on the Holy Spirit with v. 3: no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit (CCC 683). It teaches that charisms, whether extraordinary or simple and humble, are graces of the Holy Spirit that benefit the Church, and that they must be received with gratitude and tested by the pastors of the Church, with charity as the true measure (CCC 799–801). The Second Vatican Council says the Spirit distributes special graces among the faithful of every rank (Lumen Gentium 12).

r.h: Another Advocate, to be with you for ever
set: These words belong to Jesus' farewell discourse at the Last Supper (John 13–17). He has washed the disciples' feet, foretold Judas' betrayal and Peter's denial, and told them he is going to the Father. They are troubled. Into their fear he speaks a promise: they will not be left alone. The Spirit is promised five times in these chapters (14:16–17; 14:26; 15:26; 16:7–11; 16:13–15).
str: v. 15: love shown in keeping the commandments.
vv. 16–17: another Advocate, the Spirit of truth.
vv. 18–20: “I will not leave you orphaned; I am coming to you.”
v. 21: love, obedience and revelation.
vv. 22–24: Judas' question and Jesus' answer: we will make our home with them.
kw: Literally “one called to the side” of another: a helper, defender, counsellor or comforter. Jesus says “another” Advocate, because he himself has been the first; 1 John 2:1 calls Jesus our paraklētos with the Father.
Disciples were often called the “children” of their teacher (13:33). Jesus will not leave his own like children without a father.
The same word as the “dwelling places” in the Father's house (14:2). There the disciples go to the Father; here the Father and the Son come to the disciple. Heaven begins in the heart that loves.
vv: If you love me, you will keep my commandments.
Love is not only a feeling; it is shown in faithfulness. And keeping his word is itself a fruit of love.
And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, to be with you forever.
The Son asks, the Father gives, the Spirit comes. The three Persons of the Trinity appear together in one sentence.
I will not leave you orphaned; I am coming to you.
Jesus comes to his disciples in his Resurrection, in the Spirit and at the end of time. All three are in view.
and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them.

The goal of the whole Christian life: the indwelling of the Holy Trinity in the soul. Judas (not Iscariot) asked why Jesus would show himself to them and not to the world. The answer: he shows himself to those who love.
ch: The Catechism explains the name Paraclete as “he who is called to one's side” and notes that Jesus calls the Spirit “another Paraclete” (CCC 692, 243). It quotes v. 23 to say that the ultimate end of the whole divine economy is that God's creatures enter into the perfect unity of the Trinity, and that even now we are called to be a dwelling for the Holy Trinity (CCC 260). Pentecost is not only an event in Jerusalem long ago. It is the beginning of God's life in each believer.

qa: Were the tongues at Pentecost foreign languages or a kind of ecstatic speech?

In Acts 2 Luke clearly means real languages, understood by people from many nations (2:6–11). Paul in 1 Corinthians 14 speaks of a gift of tongues that no one understood without an interpreter. The two are related but not the same. In both cases the Spirit is the giver, and in both the gift is meant to build up the Church.
If the Spirit is “another” Advocate, is he less than Jesus?

No. The Church confesses that the Holy Spirit is one God with the Father and the Son, “with the Father and the Son he is worshipped and glorified”, as the Nicene Creed says. “Another” means a distinct Person, not a lesser one. Jesus was the Advocate visible among the disciples; the Spirit is the Advocate within them.
Are gifts like healing and prophecy still given today?

Yes. The Catechism teaches that charisms, extraordinary or simple and humble, continue to be given for the good of the Church (CCC 799–800). Their genuineness is discerned by the Church, and charity remains the greatest gift (1 Corinthians 13; CCC 800–801). Most gifts are quiet: a catechist's patience, a parent's wisdom, a gift for consoling the sick.
rite: On this Sunday our Church celebrates the Pentecost service of kneeling. In three parts the Church kneels and prays to the Father, to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, asking the Spirit to come upon the people as on the apostles. The season of Qyomtho ends and the season of Pentecost begins. In the Syriac tradition the Spirit is also at the heart of every Holy Qurbono: in the invocation of the Holy Spirit (the epiclesis) the priest prays that the Spirit may come upon the bread and wine and make them the Body and Blood of Christ. In our Church the newly baptized are anointed with holy Myron at once, so that each of us received the Spirit as a gift from the first day of our Christian life.
study: Ezekiel speaks of a heart of stone. Where in my heart do I still need God to give me a heart of flesh?
What gift has the Spirit given me “for the common good”, and how am I using it in my family and parish?
Jesus says the Father and he will make their home with those who love him. How can I make room for that guest this week?
Moses wished that all God's people were prophets. How can our family speak of “God's deeds of power” to those around us?

lead: The day after Pentecost the readings turn from the gift of the Spirit to the mission it brings. Paul asks the Philippians to live “in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ”, standing firm in one spirit. In Matthew, Jesus sends out the Twelve with the words: “You received without payment; give without payment.” The key words are worthy and sent.

r.h: Live in a manner worthy of the gospel
set: Paul writes from prison to a church he loves. Philippi was a Roman colony (Acts 16:12), proud of its Roman citizenship. In chapter 1 Paul tells the Philippians that his chains have helped the Gospel (1:12–14) and that for him “living is Christ and dying is gain” (1:21). Today's verses begin the main exhortation of the letter. The Philippians faced opposition, and Paul wants them united and unafraid.
str: v. 27: live worthily of the Gospel, standing firm, striving together.
v. 28: do not be intimidated by opponents.
vv. 29–30: suffering for Christ is a gift, and Paul shares the same struggle.
kw: Literally “live as citizens”. In a Roman colony the word had weight. Paul says later, “our citizenship is in heaven” (3:20). Christians live in their town as citizens of another homeland, and that shapes how they behave.
A word from the games: athletes competing together as one team. The faith of the Gospel is not a private race but a team effort.
From charis, grace. Paul says that suffering for Christ, like believing in him, is a grace given. This is not love of pain; it is sharing the path of the Lord.
vv: Only, live your life in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ,
“Only”: of all the things Paul could ask, this one thing matters. The Gospel is not only to be believed but to be lived.
For he has graciously granted you the privilege not only of believing in Christ, but of suffering for him as well
Faith itself is a gift of grace, and so is the strength to suffer for Christ. Both come from the same giver.
ch: The Church reads this passage as a call to a life that matches the faith we profess. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the laity are called to be witnesses in the world, making Christ known by the testimony of their lives (Lumen Gentium 31; 35). The Catechism reminds us that the faithful must not be ashamed of bearing witness to the Lord (CCC 2471–2472). After Pentecost, the Spirit gives the strength for this witness.

r.h: You received without payment; give without payment
set: Matthew 10 is the second of the five great discourses in Matthew's Gospel, the missionary discourse. Jesus has just named the twelve apostles (10:1–4), after seeing the crowds “like sheep without a shepherd” (9:36). Now he sends them out with instructions. They are to do what he himself has been doing: preach the Kingdom, heal the sick and cast out demons (chapters 8–9).
str: vv. 5–6: the first mission is to the lost sheep of Israel.
vv. 7–8: preach and heal; give as a gift.
vv. 9–10: travel light and trust.
vv. 11–15: staying in homes; peace given or returned; shaking off the dust.
kw: The word means “as a gift”. The apostles have received the Kingdom, the power to heal and the call itself as gifts. They must not sell what they were given.

Behind it is the Hebrew shalom, the everyday greeting that also means wholeness and blessing from God. The disciples' peace is not empty words; it is a real gift that rests on a house, or returns to them.
vv: but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
This first mission follows the order of God's plan: the promises were made first to Israel. After the Resurrection the risen Lord widens it to “all nations” (28:19).
You received without payment; give without payment.
The whole of Christian ministry in one sentence. Whatever we have received of God, we hold in trust for others.
for laborers deserve their food.
Jesus asks the apostles to trust God and the hospitality of others. Paul cites the same principle for the support of those who preach the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14).
If anyone will not welcome you or listen to your words, shake off the dust from your feet as you leave that house or town.
A prophetic sign, not a curse. It says: we have done our part; the responsibility now rests with you. Paul and Barnabas did this at Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:51).
ch: The Church sees in this sending the beginning of her own mission. The Catechism teaches that the Lord gave his community a structure that will remain until the Kingdom is fully achieved, beginning with the choice of the Twelve with Peter as their head (CCC 765). The Church also takes “give without payment” seriously in her law: the minister should ask nothing for the sacraments beyond the offerings fixed by the competent authority, and the poor must not be deprived of them (CCC 2122).

qa: Why does Jesus tell the Twelve not to go to the Gentiles and Samaritans?

This first mission keeps to the order of God's promises: to Israel first. It is not a rejection of others. In Matthew itself the Magi come from the East (2:1–12), Jesus heals a Roman centurion's servant (8:5–13), and the risen Lord sends the apostles to all nations (28:19). God's faithfulness to Israel is the ground of his mercy to the nations.
study: What have I received from God without payment that I can give to someone this week?
Paul asks for a life “worthy of the gospel”. In what one part of my life is my witness weakest?

lead: Both readings show a God who comes down to seek us. Hebrews says that the Son shared our flesh and blood so that he might become “a merciful and faithful high priest” and help those who are tested. In Luke a woman lights a lamp, sweeps the house and searches for one lost coin, and there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. The key words are shared and found.

r.h: He shared our flesh and blood
set: The first chapters of Hebrews show that the Son is greater than the angels (chapter 1). Then the author faces a question: if the Son is so great, why did he become man and suffer? He answers from Psalm 8: the Son was made “for a little while lower than the angels” so that “by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone” (2:9). Today's verses explain why this was fitting. This is the first time Hebrews calls Jesus “high priest”, the great theme of the letter.
str: vv. 14–15: he shared flesh and blood to destroy the power of death and the devil.
v. 16: he came to help the descendants of Abraham, not angels.
vv. 17–18: like us in every respect, a merciful and faithful high priest who helps those who are tested.
kw: The children “share” flesh and blood; the Son “likewise shared” the same things. The word for fellowship, koinōnia, is in the root. God enters into fellowship with our human condition.
a merciful and faithful high priest
Merciful toward us, faithful toward God. A high priest stands between God and the people. Jesus can do this perfectly because he is both.
to make a sacrifice of atonement
The verb of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), when the high priest entered the Holy of Holies with blood. Hebrews will show that Christ fulfils this once for all with his own blood (9:11–14).
vv: Since, therefore, the children share flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared the same things,
The Incarnation is not a disguise. The Son took a real human nature, body and soul, and lived a real human life.
and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by the fear of death.
Fear of death can rule a whole life. Christ went through death and broke its power, so that his own need not live as slaves of that fear.
Because he himself was tested by what he suffered, he is able to help those who are being tested.
Jesus knows our trials from within. Hebrews later adds that he was tested in every way as we are, “yet without sin” (4:15).
ch: The Church reads this passage as a key to the Incarnation and the priesthood of Christ. St Gregory of Nazianzus wrote that what was not assumed was not healed (Letter 101, in substance): the Son took all that is human in order to save all that is human. The Catechism teaches that Christ is the one high priest, in whom everything the priesthood of the Old Covenant prefigured is fulfilled (CCC 1544), and that he conquered the tempter for us, as one able to sympathize with our weaknesses (CCC 540).

r.h: The woman who searches for the lost coin
set: Luke 15 holds three parables of the lost: the sheep, the coin and the son. They answer the grumbling of some Pharisees and scribes who said, “This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them” (15:2). The parable of the coin is found only in Luke. It stands between the shepherd and the father, and here the one who searches is a woman.
str: v. 8: one coin lost; lamp, broom and careful search.
v. 9: found; friends and neighbours called to rejoice.
v. 10: so there is joy before the angels over one sinner who repents.
kw: A Greek silver coin, roughly a day's wage for a labourer. For a poor woman ten coins could be all her savings.
Literally “change one's mind”: a turning of the whole person back to God. In the parable the coin does nothing; the woman does all the searching. Repentance is first of all being found.
vv: does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?
Houses of poor families often had few windows and earthen floors. Finding a small coin meant patient, careful work. God searches for us with the same patience.
Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.
Joy is meant to be shared. Heaven's joy over a sinner who returns is a feast to which the whole community is invited.
Just so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.
“In the presence of the angels” is a reverent way of speaking of God himself. It is God who rejoices.
ch: The Church hears in this parable the heart of God who seeks sinners. The Catechism teaches that Jesus invites sinners to the table of the Kingdom and that he speaks of the boundless mercy of the Father for them and of the joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (CCC 545). Some Fathers, among them St Gregory the Great (Homilies on the Gospels 34, in substance), saw in the woman the Wisdom of God, and in the lamp the light of God shining in Christ's humanity. The sacrament of Penance is the place where the lost coin is found again.

qa: If Jesus was tested like us, could he have sinned?

The Church teaches that Jesus was truly tempted but was without sin (Hebrews 4:15). His temptations were real, not play-acting, but his will was perfectly united with the Father's. Because he never gave in, he knows the full weight of temptation better than we do, and he can help us in ours.
study: What fear has the strongest grip on my life, and how does the victory of Christ over death speak to it?
Is there someone in my family or parish who is “lost” and whom I could help God to search for?

lead: Three days after Pentecost our Church remembers, by an old tradition, the first Holy Qurbono offered by Mar Yaqob Shleeha, James the brother of the Lord and first bishop of Jerusalem. Both readings take us back to the night when it all began. Paul hands on to the Corinthians what he himself received: the Lord Jesus took bread and the cup and said, “Do this in remembrance of me.” Luke shows the same night from inside the upper room, where Jesus says, “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” The key words are hand on, remembrance and covenant.

r.h: What I received from the Lord
set: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus (16:8), around AD 53–55. The church in Corinth was gifted but divided, and the divisions showed even at the Lord's Supper. When they gathered, some went ahead with their own meal while others, the poor, went hungry (11:20–22). Paul does not answer first with a new rule. He reminds them what the Supper is.

These four verses are the oldest written account of the Last Supper that we have, older than the Gospels in their written form. Paul had taught it to the Corinthians when he founded their church, around AD 50, and he says that it came to him as a tradition from the Lord himself.
str: v. 23a: the chain of tradition: received from the Lord, handed on to you.
vv. 23b–24: the night of betrayal; the bread, the thanksgiving, “This is my body”.
v. 25: the cup after supper: the new covenant in my blood.
v. 26: Paul's comment: every Supper proclaims the Lord's death until he comes.
¶ In the verses that follow Paul draws the lesson: whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup in an unworthy manner will be answerable for the body and blood of the Lord (11:27–29).
kw: The pair of words used for passing on a sacred teaching from teacher to disciple. Paul uses the same pair in 15:3 for the Gospel of the Resurrection. The Eucharist reached Corinth as a gift handed on, not as something the community made up. There is a play on words too: the night when Jesus “was betrayed” uses the same verb. On the night he was handed over, he handed himself over for us.

More than a memory in the mind. In the Bible, to remember before God makes the saving event present. Israel kept the Passover as “a day of remembrance” (Exodus 12:14), and each generation was to tell what the Lord had done for it.
The word used for preaching the Gospel. The Supper itself is a proclamation: it announces the Lord's death as the source of life, and it looks forward to his coming.
vv: the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread,
Paul names the night, not only the meal. The Eucharist is bound to the Passion. It comes from the hour when one disciple handed Jesus over and Jesus gave himself up for all.
“This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

“For you” gives the meaning of the gift: a body given up on behalf of others. Among the four accounts of the Supper, only Paul and Luke keep the command “Do this”, which the Church has always understood as given to the apostles and to those who follow them in their ministry.
This cup is the new covenant in my blood.

Jeremiah promised a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34). At Sinai Moses sprinkled the people with “the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8). Jesus joins the two: the covenant is new, and it is sealed in his own blood.
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
The Supper looks two ways: back to the Cross and forward to the Lord's return. The first Christians prayed in Aramaic, Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!” (16:22).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Eucharist is the memorial of Christ's Passover. In the liturgy this memorial is not only the recalling of past events: the sacrifice that Christ offered once for all on the Cross remains ever present (CCC 1362–1364). The Catechism points to this passage for the Lord's command to repeat his words and actions “until he comes” (CCC 1341). With the Council of Trent it teaches that at the Last Supper Christ instituted the Eucharist and made his apostles priests of the New Testament (CCC 1337). Paul's own concern is also the Church's: the Body of Christ received at the altar cannot be separated from his body the community, and above all from its poorest members. The Eucharist commits us to the poor (CCC 1397).

r.h: I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you
set: Luke places the Supper at the hour of the Passover meal (22:7–13). Jesus has sent Peter and John to prepare it in a large upper room. Luke's account is the longest of the four, because after the meal Jesus goes on speaking with the apostles at the table (22:21–38).

Luke's words over the bread and the cup are very close to Paul's: both have “for you”, “Do this in remembrance of me” and “the new covenant in my blood”. Scholars commonly note that Luke and Paul share one form of the tradition, and Mark and Matthew another. Luke is named as Paul's companion in Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 24.
str: v. 14: the hour comes; Jesus takes his place with the apostles.
vv. 15–16: his great desire, and the Passover fulfilled in the kingdom of God.
vv. 17–18: a first cup, shared among them.
v. 19: the bread: my body given for you.
v. 20: the cup after supper: the new covenant in my blood, poured out for you.
kw: Literally “with desire I have desired”. The Greek copies a Hebrew way of speaking that doubles a word to make it strong. It shows the heart of Jesus as he goes to his Passion: he does not only accept this meal, he has longed for it.

The feast of Israel's deliverance from Egypt (Exodus 12). Jesus will not eat it again “until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God”. The old feast is not thrown aside; it reaches its fulfilment in him. Paul calls Christ “our paschal lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7).
A word of sacrifice, used of blood poured out at the altar. The Greek is in the present tense: the offering of the Cross is already present at the table.
vv: When the hour came, he took his place at the table, and the apostles with him.
Luke gives the Supper a solemn beginning. The word “apostles”, those who are sent, reminds us that this meal is given to men who will be sent out.
I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer;
Only Luke records this saying. Before we desire the Eucharist, Christ has desired to give himself to us.
“This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

Textual note: a few ancient witnesses, chiefly one Greek manuscript (Codex Bezae) and some Old Latin copies, stop after “This is my body”. Almost all manuscripts have the longer text, and the NRSV and other modern editions print it, as the Church's lectionary does.
This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.

Luke mentions two cups (vv. 17 and 20). The Passover meal, as later Jewish sources describe it, had several cups of wine. Many scholars think the first cup belongs to the Passover rite, and the second, “after supper”, is the cup of the new covenant.
ch: The Church reads this account as the institution of the Eucharist and of the priesthood that serves it. The Catechism says that by celebrating the Last Supper with his apostles in the course of the Passover meal, Jesus gave the Jewish Passover its definitive meaning (CCC 1340). St Ignatius of Antioch, whom our Church honours as Mar Ignatius Noorono, wrote that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins and which the Father raised up (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 7, in substance). The Church takes the Lord at his word, “This is my body”: under the signs of bread and wine Christ is truly, really and substantially present (CCC 1374).

qa: Which James is remembered today?

James “the Lord's brother” (Galatians 1:19), who led the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; 21:18). He is not James the son of Zebedee, whose death by the sword is told in Acts 12:2 and whom our Church honoured on 30 April. The Latin tradition has usually identified the brother of the Lord with the apostle James the son of Alphaeus; Eastern traditions often keep them apart. The question has never been settled with certainty. “Brother” in the Bible can mean a close relative, and the Church holds that Mary remained ever virgin (CCC 500).
Did Mar Yaqob write the Anaphora that bears his name?

The Anaphora of St James carries his name because it comes from the Church of Jerusalem, where he was the first bishop. Many scholars think its present text took shape in Jerusalem in the fourth century, from older roots, and was then carried to Antioch and beyond. The name honours its source: the church that first devoted itself to “the breaking of bread and the prayers” after Pentecost (Acts 2:42).
rite: Today our Church keeps the memory of the first Holy Qurbono offered by Mar Yaqob, the brother of the Lord. In the West Syriac tradition his name stands first among the anaphoras: the Anaphora of St James is honoured as the chief one, after whose pattern many others were composed. When the priest repeats the words of the Lord over the bread and the cup and the people answer “Amen”, we stand in the chain that Paul describes: what was received from the Lord is handed on. This week after Pentecost also reminds us that the Spirit who came upon the apostles is the same Spirit called down upon the gifts at every Holy Qurbono.
study: Paul says he handed on what he had received. Who handed on the faith of the Holy Qurbono to me, and to whom am I handing it on?
Jesus “eagerly desired” to eat this Passover with his apostles. How can I prepare to meet that desire next Sunday?
Paul links the Lord's Supper with care for the poor of the community. Who goes hungry near my parish table?

lead: Today our Church honours the four Evangelists together: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. The Epistle traces the chain by which faith reaches anyone at all: someone is sent, someone proclaims, someone hears, someone believes and calls on the Lord. “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!” The Gospel is the last page of Matthew, where the risen Lord sends the eleven to all nations and promises, “I am with you always.” The four Evangelists stand in that sending: what the apostles preached, they wrote down for every generation. The key words are sent, hear and with you.

r.h: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news
set: Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, around AD 57, to a church he had not yet visited. Chapters 9–11 wrestle with a question that grieved him deeply: why had most of his own people, Israel, not accepted Jesus as the Messiah? He begins with “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” (9:2). He ends by saying that “all Israel will be saved” (11:26) and that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29).

Just before today's verses Paul has quoted the prophet Joel: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved” (10:13). Now he traces, link by link, the chain that makes such calling possible.
str: vv. 14–15: the chain: call, believe, hear, proclaim, be sent; Isaiah 52:7.
vv. 16–17: not all have obeyed; faith comes from what is heard (Isaiah 53:1).
v. 18: the message has gone out to all the earth (Psalm 19:4).
vv. 19–20: Moses and Isaiah: God found by those who did not seek him (Deuteronomy 32:21; Isaiah 65:1).

¶ The next verse (10:21) shows God holding out his hands “all day long” to his people. The passage ends not in rejection but in God's patience, and chapter 11 opens: “has God rejected his people? By no means!”
kw: From this verb comes the word apostle. Preaching in the Church is not self-appointed: “how are they to proclaim him unless they are sent?” The Evangelists wrote within this sending, and their books carry the preaching of the apostles.
The verb of Isaiah 52:7 in the Greek Old Testament, used of the messenger running over the mountains to Jerusalem to say, “Your God reigns.” Our word Evangelist comes from the same root.

The same word means both the act of hearing and the message that is heard. Faith begins as an answer to a word that comes to us from outside. Paul adds “through the word of Christ”: the message is about Christ, and in it Christ himself speaks.
vv: And how are they to proclaim him unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”
In Isaiah the feet belong to a runner bringing news of peace to Jerusalem after the exile. They are beautiful not for their shape but for the news they carry, and for the long road they have walked.
So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.
Faith is personal, but it is never private in its origin. No one gives it to himself. It comes through a voice: a parent, a catechist, a priest, a book of the Gospels read aloud.
Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.

Psalm 19 says this of the heavens, which declare God's glory without speech. Paul applies it to the apostles' preaching. He quotes the Greek Old Testament, “their voice”; the Hebrew text has “their line”.
I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.
From Isaiah 65:1. Paul reads it of the Gentiles who came to faith without having looked for it. God goes ahead of every search.
ch: The Church reads this passage as the charter of her preaching. The Catechism quotes verses 14–15 to show that no one can give himself the mandate to preach the Gospel: the minister of Christ is sent and speaks with an authority he has received (CCC 875). The Second Vatican Council teaches that among all the Scriptures the Gospels have a special place, because they are the principal witness to the life and teaching of the incarnate Word, and that the Church has always held that the four Gospels are of apostolic origin (Dei Verbum 18). Paul's sorrow for his own people is also the Church's: God has not rejected Israel, and the Church relates to the Jewish people as to those to whom God first spoke (CCC 839).

r.h: Go therefore and make disciples of all nations
set: These are the last verses of Matthew's Gospel. On Easter morning the risen Lord met the women and gave them a message for “my brothers”: go to Galilee, and there they will see me (28:10). Galilee is where Jesus began his preaching, “Galilee of the Gentiles” (4:15). Matthew does not describe the Ascension. His Gospel ends with a promise of presence.
Matthew's Gospel began with the name Emmanuel, “God is with us” (1:23). It ends with “I am with you always”. The whole book lies between these two sayings.
str: v. 16: the eleven go to the mountain in Galilee.
v. 17: worship, and doubt.
v. 18: all authority given to Jesus.
vv. 19–20a: go, make disciples, baptize, teach.
v. 20b: I am with you always.
kw: The one main command in the sentence; going, baptizing and teaching serve it. A disciple is a learner who follows the master and lives with him. The mission is not only to win agreement but to form lives.

During his ministry Jesus sent the Twelve first to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (10:6). Now the circle opens to every people. Israel is not left out. The promise to Abraham, that in him “all the families of the earth shall be blessed”, is reaching its goal (Genesis 12:3).
Baptism is “in the name”, singular, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. The Greek suggests being plunged into, and belonging to, the one God who is three persons.
vv: When they saw him, they worshiped him; but some doubted.

Matthew is honest. On the mountain of the risen Lord, worship and hesitation stand side by side. The verb for doubt is the one Jesus used to Peter sinking in the waves: “why did you doubt?” (14:31). Jesus does not send the hesitant away. In the next verse he comes near to them.
All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.

Daniel saw one like a son of man, to whom was given dominion over all peoples (Daniel 7:13–14). The risen Jesus speaks as that Son of Man. The mission rests on his authority, not on the strength of the eleven.
Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
The clearest naming of the Trinity in the Gospels. The early Church baptized with these words; the Didache, a very early Christian handbook, already gives them.
And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.
Not “I will be” but “I am”. Many readers hear in it an echo of God's name revealed to Moses, “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14). The Church goes out with the Lord already at her side.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses as the origin of the Church's missionary mandate (CCC 849), and teaches that we are baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, not in their names, for there is only one God (CCC 233). St Irenaeus of Lyons, writing around AD 180, held that there can be neither more nor fewer than four Gospels, as there are four winds and four quarters of the world, and he linked them with the four living creatures around God's throne (Against Heresies 3.11.8, in substance; Revelation 4:6–7). St Jerome later gave the symbols that Christian art still uses: the man for Matthew, the lion for Mark, the ox for Luke and the eagle for John.

qa: Why four Gospels and not one?

The early Church received four written witnesses to the one Gospel of Jesus Christ, each rooted in the apostles' preaching. Their differences in order and detail are like four witnesses describing the same events. In the second century Tatian wove them into a single account, the Diatessaron, which was read in Syriac-speaking churches for a long time; Mar Aprem wrote a commentary on it. In the end the Church kept the four, because each brings out something of the one Lord in its own way (Dei Verbum 18–19; CCC 125–127).
Who were the Evangelists?

Matthew and John are counted by the Church's tradition among the Twelve. Early writers link Mark with Peter and Luke with Paul. Many scholars today think the Gospels as we have them were written down between about AD 65 and 100, drawing on the preaching and tradition of the apostles. The Church holds them to be of apostolic origin and to hand on faithfully what Jesus really did and taught (Dei Verbum 18–19).
rite: Our Church honours the four Evangelists on one day. In the Holy Qurbono the reading of the Gospel is surrounded with signs of honour: lighted candles, incense, and the people standing to listen. The Gospel is announced with the name of the apostle or evangelist who wrote it, and the people answer with praise to the Lord who sent him. The Syriac Churches once read the four Gospels woven into one, in the Diatessaron, and then returned to the four separate books.
