Today we thank God for the four voices through which the one Gospel has reached Kerala and our own homes.
study: Paul says that faith comes from what is heard. Through whose voice did I first hear the Gospel, and have I thanked God for that person?
Matthew is honest that “some doubted”. What doubt do I bring to the Lord, and what does it mean to me that he still comes near?
Which Gospel do I know best, and which least? How could our family read one Gospel through, slowly, in the coming months?

lead: The first Friday after Pentecost is kept in our Church as Golden Friday. It recalls the first sign of the apostles that Acts tells in detail after the Spirit came: Peter and John at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and Peter's words, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you.” The Epistle names the gift that is worth more than gold: love, without which tongues, prophecy and even martyrdom are nothing. The Gospel warns of riches that make it hard to enter the kingdom, and promises that “for God all things are possible”. Today is also the memory of St Helena, the mother of the emperor Constantine.

The three readings answer one question: what does the Church really have to give? Not silver and gold, but the name of Jesus, the love poured out by the Spirit, and the treasure of the kingdom that only God can open to us. The key words are the name, love and possible.

r.h: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk
set: Acts 2 ends with a picture of the first community in Jerusalem: devoted to the apostles' teaching, the breaking of bread and the prayers, and going to the temple together day by day (2:42–46). Many “wonders and signs” were done by the apostles (2:43), and chapter 3 now tells one of them at length. The first believers still prayed in the temple with their fellow Jews; faith in Jesus did not mean leaving the God of Israel.

The ninth hour, three in the afternoon, was the time of the evening sacrifice and of prayer in the temple. No other ancient source calls a gate “the Beautiful Gate”. Many identify it with the great bronze gate on the east side of the inner courts, but its place is not certain.
str: vv. 1–3: Peter and John go up to pray; the lame man asks for alms.
vv. 4–5: “Look at us”: he expects money.
v. 6: “I have no silver or gold”: the name of Jesus.
vv. 7–8: Peter raises him up; he walks and leaps and praises God.
vv. 9–10: the people recognize him and are filled with wonder.
¶ Peter's sermon follows at once (3:11–26): “by faith in his name, his name itself has made this man strong” (3:16).
kw: In the Bible the name stands for the person and his power. The apostles do not heal by their own power or holiness (3:12) but in the name of Jesus. The name given by the angel, Yeshua, means “the Lord saves”.
The verb used for the Resurrection of Jesus. The healing of a man lame from birth is a small Easter: the risen Lord raises up one who had never walked.
Isaiah promised for the day of God's coming: “then the lame shall leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6). Luke lets us hear that the promise is being kept.
vv: Peter looked intently at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.”
The man was used to people hurrying past. Before any miracle there is a look. Charity begins by seeing the person.
I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk.
Peter is not ashamed to be poor. He gives what he has received. The man asked for a coin and received his life back.
And he took him by the right hand and raised him up; and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.

Luke, whom Paul calls “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), notes the feet and ankles. Peter does with his hand what Jesus once did for Peter's mother-in-law: “took her by the hand and lifted her up” (Mark 1:31).
he entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
The man who sat outside the gate every day now goes in with the apostles to pray. The first thing he does with his new strength is to praise God.
ch: The Church sees in this scene what she is meant to be. She must care for the poor, and she does. But first she gives what she has received, the name and the life of Jesus. The Catechism teaches that after the Resurrection it is the name of Jesus that fully shows the power of God (CCC 434; see Acts 3:16). A well-known story tells that a pope once showed St Thomas Aquinas the treasures of the Church and said, “The Church can no longer say, ‘Silver and gold I have none.’” Thomas answered, “Neither can she say, ‘Rise and walk.’” The story may be a legend, but it has been told for centuries because it makes the point well.

r.h: If I do not have love, I am nothing
set: In chapters 12–14 Paul answers the Corinthians' questions about spiritual gifts. Some prized speaking in tongues above everything else. Paul has just said that the Church is one body with many members, each with its own gift (12:12–31). Before he gives rules for using the gifts (chapter 14), he shows them “a still more excellent way” (12:31).
This chapter is often read at weddings, and it fits them well. But Paul first wrote it for a quarrelling community, to show what gives every gift its worth.
str: vv. 1–3: without love, tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith and even self-sacrifice are nothing.
vv. 4–6: what love does and does not do.
¶ The reading stops at v. 6. The chapter goes on: love “bears all things” and “never ends” (13:7–8), and of faith, hope and love, “the greatest of these is love” (13:13).
kw: The New Testament's chosen word for the love that God has shown in Christ, the love that “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5). It is not first a feeling but a way of acting for the good of the other.

Literally “is long-tempered”, slow to anger. In the Greek Old Testament the same family of words describes God himself: “slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love” (Exodus 34:6). Patient love is God's own way with us.
vv: If I speak in the tongues of mortals and of angels, but do not have love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.
Corinth was famous for its bronze work. A gong makes a great noise and has nothing inside. The most beautiful speech without love is only noise.
If I give away all my possessions, and if I hand over my body so that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing.

Textual note: the Greek manuscripts differ here by a single letter. Some read “so that I may boast”, which the NRSV follows; others read “to be burned”, which many older translations follow, as does the POC. Either way, even the greatest sacrifice without love gains nothing.
Love is patient; love is kind; love is not envious or boastful or arrogant
Paul describes love by verbs, by what it does. Several things that love is not are faults he has already named in the Corinthians: jealousy (3:3) and arrogance (4:18; 5:2).
it does not rejoice in wrongdoing, but rejoices in the truth.
Love is not softness about evil. It cannot be glad when wrong is done, even to an enemy. It is glad when the truth comes out.
ch: The Catechism calls charity the theological virtue by which we love God above all things for his own sake, and our neighbour as ourselves for the love of God (CCC 1822). It quotes this chapter at length and calls charity the form of all the virtues (CCC 1825–1827). St Augustine, preaching on the First Letter of John, gave his famous saying, “Love, and do what you will”: if the root of love is within, nothing but good can grow from it (Homilies on 1 John 7.8, in substance). He did not mean that anything goes. He meant that true love of God shapes every act, even correction.

r.h: For God all things are possible
set: Just before this a rich young man asked Jesus what good deed he must do to have eternal life. Jesus told him to keep the commandments, and then to sell his possessions, give to the poor and follow him. “When the young man heard this word, he went away grieving, for he had many possessions” (19:22). Today's Gospel is what Jesus says to the disciples as the young man walks away.
str: vv. 23–24: hard for the rich: the camel and the needle.
vv. 25–26: “Then who can be saved?” For God all things are possible.
vv. 27–29: Peter: we have left everything; the twelve thrones and the hundredfold.
v. 30: the first will be last, and the last first.
kw: The largest animal in the land, through the smallest opening. It is a deliberate exaggeration, a way of saying “impossible”. The story of a small gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye has no ancient evidence behind it, and it softens a saying that Jesus meant to startle.

Literally “new birth”. Here it means the renewal of the whole creation at the end, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his glory. The same word is used of Baptism in Titus 3:5, “the water of rebirth”.
vv: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God.
Jesus does not say that the rich are worse than others. He says that riches can hold the heart so tightly that it cannot pass through the narrow door.
Then who can be saved?
In much of the Old Testament wealth was seen as a sign of God's blessing (Deuteronomy 28:1–14). If even the rich find it so hard, the disciples think, what hope is there for anyone?
For mortals it is impossible, but for God all things are possible.
The answer is not that salvation is easy, but that it is God's gift. The angel said the same to Mary: “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37).
everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or fields, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold, and will inherit eternal life.
“For my name's sake”: the same name that healed the lame man in Acts. Mark adds that the hundredfold comes “with persecutions” (Mark 10:30).
ch: The Church does not condemn wealth as such, but she warns that riches can seize the heart. The Catechism teaches that Jesus enjoins his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone, and that detachment from riches is necessary for entrance into the Kingdom (CCC 2544). It teaches that the goods of creation are meant for the whole human race (CCC 2402–2406) and speaks of the Church's love of preference for the poor (CCC 2448). St Clement of Alexandria wrote a whole treatise on this Gospel, Who Is the Rich Man That Is Saved?, teaching that what must be given up is the soul's clinging to wealth, so that riches may serve others (in substance).

qa: Why is it called Golden Friday?

The name comes from Peter's words, “I have no silver or gold.” The apostles had no gold to give, and what they gave was richer than gold. In our tradition this first Friday after Pentecost honours that first great sign of the apostles after the Spirit came.
Is the hundredfold a promise of wealth?

No. Mark's version says it comes “with persecutions” (Mark 10:30). It is the new family of the Church: brothers, sisters and mothers in faith, homes opened in hospitality, and above all eternal life. The fishermen who left their nets received the whole Church as their family.
Does 1 Corinthians 13 mean that faith matters less than love?

No. Paul says that faith, hope and love all abide (13:13). Love is the greatest because it alone remains in heaven, where faith becomes sight and hope is fulfilled. Faith without love is dead, and love is the life of faith (CCC 1814–1815, 1826).
rite: Golden Friday belongs to the first week of the season of Pentecost in our calendar. It sets the healing at the Beautiful Gate at the start of the season of Pentecost, as a sign that the Spirit has been given for the healing of the world. Today the Eastern Churches also honour St Helena, with her son Constantine. Helena, a woman of humble birth, became the mother of the first Christian emperor. In her old age, around 326–328, she went on pilgrimage to the Holy Land, and churches were built at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives. From the end of the fourth century writers such as St Ambrose told that she found the Cross of the Lord in Jerusalem (in substance). She is a fitting saint for Golden Friday: an empress who used her wealth to honour the places of the Lord's life and to help the poor.
study: Peter said, “what I have I give you.” What have I received from God that I could give to someone today, apart from money?
Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–6 and put my own name in place of “love”. Which line is hardest to say truthfully?
What possession or comfort holds my heart most tightly? What would it mean to trust that “for God all things are possible”?
St Helena used her wealth for the Lord's places and the poor. How does our family decide what to give?

lead: On the Saturday after Pentecost the Epistle speaks of the Spirit writing on human hearts: “you are a letter of Christ... written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God.” The Gospel of the ten bridesmaids asks whether the lamp of that life is still burning when the bridegroom comes. Today is also the memory of St Rita of Cascia, wife, mother, widow and nun, who kept her lamp lit through great sorrow. The key words are letter, Spirit and oil.

r.h: Written not with ink but with the Spirit
set: Some newcomers in Corinth carried letters of recommendation and compared themselves favourably with Paul. Paul refuses to play that game: his only letter is the community itself. He then compares his ministry with that of Moses, drawing on Exodus 34:29–35, where Moses' face shone after he had spoken with God, so that the people “were afraid to come near him” (Exodus 34:30).
str: vv. 1–3: you are our letter, written by the Spirit on hearts.
vv. 4–6: our competence is from God, who made us ministers of a new covenant.
vv. 7–11: if the old ministry came with glory, much more the ministry of the Spirit.
kw: Christ is the author, Paul the one who prepared and delivered it, the Spirit the ink, and the hearts of the Corinthians the page. Jeremiah promised that God would write his law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33), and Ezekiel that he would give “a heart of flesh” in place of stone (Ezekiel 36:26).

Paul does not set Scripture against inner feeling. The “letter” is the law written outside us, holy in itself but without power to give the life it commands. The Spirit writes God's will within and gives the strength to live it.
vv: You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all;
A changed community is the best proof of a true ministry. People who never open the Bible can still read the Christians around them.
for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

Not an attack on the Law of Moses, which Paul calls “holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). On its own a written commandment can show sin but cannot heal it. The Spirit gives the life the commandment points to.
how much more will the ministry of the Spirit come in glory?
Paul does not deny the glory of Sinai; he builds on it. The old covenant had real glory. The new has a glory that lasts.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit given to the faithful through faith in Christ, a law written within, on the heart (CCC 1965–1966). It does not abolish the Old Law but fulfils and perfects it (CCC 1967–1968). St Thomas Aquinas taught the same: the New Law is chiefly the grace of the Holy Spirit itself (in substance). Paul's reading of Moses' veil (3:12–18) is about how Christians read the Scriptures in Christ, and the Church reads it with deep respect for the Jewish people, to whom “belong the covenants” (Romans 9:4; CCC 839).

r.h: Those who were ready went with him
set: The parable belongs to Jesus' last discourse in Matthew (chapters 24–25), spoken on the Mount of Olives in the days before his Passion. After speaking of his coming at an hour no one knows, he tells three parables of the time of waiting: the bridesmaids, the talents, and the judgement of the nations. Read on the Saturday after Pentecost, the parable takes on a particular colour. In the Bible oil is a sign of the Holy Spirit, who anoints and gives light (CCC 695), and the Epistle has just spoken of the Spirit writing on our hearts.
str: vv. 1–4: ten go out to meet the bridegroom; only five bring oil.
vv. 5–7: all fall asleep; at midnight the cry wakes them.
vv. 8–9: the lamps of the foolish are going out.
vv. 10–12: those who were ready go in; the door is shut.
v. 13: the lesson: keep awake.
kw: The word used when a town went out in procession to meet an arriving king or great guest and escort him in. Paul uses it of the Church going out “to meet the Lord” at his coming (1 Thessalonians 4:17). The bridesmaids are a picture of the whole Church.
The word of the whole parable. Readiness is not something added at the last minute. It is what a person has become by the time the cry is heard.
vv: As the bridegroom was delayed, all of them became drowsy and slept.
Matthew's first readers were already living with the delay of the Lord's coming. The parable does not scold them for sleeping. It asks what they carry while they wait.
and those who were ready went with him into the wedding banquet; and the door was shut.
The joy of the feast and the seriousness of the closed door stand in one sentence. The time of preparing is now.
Truly I tell you, I do not know you.
Similar words are spoken to those who said “Lord, Lord” but did not do the Father's will (7:21–23). To be known by the Lord is to have lived with him.
ch: The Second Vatican Council takes up the last verse: since we know neither the day nor the hour, we must, as the Lord advised, watch constantly, so that we may enter with him into the marriage feast (Lumen Gentium 48; CCC 1036). St John Chrysostom saw in the oil the works of mercy, which no one can buy at the last hour (Homilies on Matthew 78, in substance). Such works are not our own achievement. They are the fruit of the Spirit in a life kept close to the Lord, and it is the Spirit who keeps the lamp burning.

qa: Does the shut door mean that God's mercy runs out?

No. God's mercy has no limit while we live, and he “is patient with you, not wanting any to perish” (2 Peter 3:9). The parable warns that the time to receive that mercy is this life. The Church teaches that each person receives his eternal recompense at death, and urges us never to put off conversion (CCC 1021–1022, 1036).
rite: St Rita (about 1381–1457) lived in Umbria in Italy. Married young to a violent husband, she bore it with patience and prayer, and he was later killed. She forgave his killers and prayed that her sons would not take revenge. After their death she entered the Augustinian convent at Cascia. She is honoured as a patron of difficult causes. Her life shows the oil of the wise bridesmaids: love kept burning through long years of sorrow.
study: If someone “read” my life this week as a letter of Christ, what would they learn about him?
Is there a conversion I keep putting off until later? What would it mean to be “ready” today?

lead: On the First Sunday after Pentecost the readings follow God's people on the road, fed and guided by him. The evening Gospel (Luke 8:4–15) is the parable of the sower: the word falls on every kind of ground, and in good soil it bears fruit “with patient endurance”. Exodus 12:31–42 tells of the night Israel went out of Egypt, “a night of vigil” for the Lord. Micah 3:8–10 shows the prophet “filled with power, with the spirit of the Lord”, who speaks the truth to rulers who build with injustice. In Jeremiah 29:10–16 God promises the exiles “a future with hope”. In Acts 17:10–15 the Jews of Beroea receive Paul's message eagerly and examine the scriptures every day to see whether these things are so.

We study three readings more closely. In Joshua the manna stops on the day Israel eats the produce of the promised land. In Galatians Paul sets the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit. In John the crowd asks for bread like the manna, and Jesus speaks of the true bread from heaven that the Father gives. The key words are bread, Spirit and believe.

r.h: The manna ceased
set: After forty years in the wilderness Israel has crossed the Jordan on dry ground (Joshua 3–4) and camped at Gilgal, on the plain near Jericho. Before any battle, two things are done. The men born in the wilderness are circumcised, so that the sign of the covenant is restored (5:2–8). Then Israel keeps the Passover, the first in the promised land.

The book of Joshua tells the entry into the land with the eyes of faith and of worship. Its story is shaped like a liturgy: the ark goes ahead, the people cross as they did at the Red Sea, stones are set up as a memorial (4:1–9), and the first act in the land is a feast of remembrance.
str: v. 9: God rolls away the disgrace of Egypt; the name Gilgal.
v. 10: the Passover on the evening of the fourteenth day, on the plains of Jericho.
v. 11: the first food from the land: unleavened cakes and parched grain.
v. 12: the manna ceases; from now on they eat the crops of Canaan.
kw: A play on words: the name Gilgal sounds like the Hebrew verb “to roll”. The place itself would remind Israel of what God did there. “The disgrace of Egypt” is the shame of slavery, now taken away.

The name comes from the question the Israelites asked when they first saw it: “What is it?” (Exodus 16:15; in Hebrew mān hû’). It fed them for forty years (Exodus 16:35). It stops on the day that the land itself can feed them.

The feast of the night of deliverance from Egypt. Israel's journey began with a Passover (Exodus 12), and the wilderness years end with one. Each new stage of life with God begins with remembering what he has done.
vv: Today I have rolled away from you the disgrace of Egypt.
“Today” is a favourite word of Deuteronomy and Joshua. God's saving act is not only a memory; it reaches the people now.
While the Israelites were camped in Gilgal they kept the passover in the evening on the fourteenth day of the month in the plains of Jericho.
The date of the first Passover (Exodus 12:6). Forty years have passed, and God's people are where the promise said they would be. Their first act is worship.
On the day after the passover, on that very day, they ate the produce of the land, unleavened cakes and parched grain.
Bread from the land they had not yet conquered, but had been given. The promised land is a gift before it is a task.
The manna ceased on the day they ate the produce of the land,
God does not stop caring for his people. He changes the way he feeds them: no longer by a daily wonder, but through the harvest and their own work.
ch: The Church has always seen the manna as a figure of the Eucharist. The Catechism names it among the Old Testament signs that the liturgy reads in the light of Christ: the manna in the desert prefigured the Eucharist, “the true bread from heaven” (CCC 1094). The manna fed Israel on the way; it ended when the people reached the land. The Eucharist is the food of the Church on her pilgrimage, the pledge of the glory to come (CCC 1402–1405), until the day when we sit at the banquet of the kingdom. Like Israel at Gilgal, the Church begins every stage of her life with a memorial of the Lord's Passover.

r.h: The fruit of the Spirit
set: Paul wrote to the churches of Galatia, in the interior of what is now Turkey, when some teachers were urging his Gentile converts to be circumcised and to keep the Mosaic law in order to belong fully to God's people. Paul answers that we are made right with God through faith in Christ, and that the Spirit has been given to us (3:1–5).

But the liberty of God's children is not licence. Just before today's reading Paul warns: “do not use your freedom as an opportunity for self-indulgence, but through love become slaves to one another” (5:13). Now he shows where such love comes from: from the Spirit.
str: vv. 16–18: live by the Spirit; Spirit and flesh are opposed.
vv. 19–21: the works of the flesh, and Paul's warning.
vv. 22–23: the fruit of the Spirit.
v. 24: those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh.
vv. 25–26: keep in step with the Spirit; no conceit or envy.
kw: Not the body as such, which God made good and which will rise. In Paul “flesh” means human nature turned in on itself and away from God. That is why the works of the flesh include not only sins of the body but also enmity, jealousy, factions and envy.

Paul speaks of the “works” (plural) of the flesh but of the “fruit” (singular) of the Spirit. Works are things we produce; fruit grows from a living root. The nine qualities are one harvest, and its first name is love.
In v. 25 a verb for walking in line, like people keeping step in a procession. Having received life from the Spirit, we are to keep in step with him day by day.
vv: Live by the Spirit, I say, and do not gratify the desires of the flesh.
Paul's first answer to temptation is not a list of rules but a way of walking. The Greek says literally “walk by the Spirit”.
By contrast, the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness,
Love comes first, and the others show what love looks like in daily life. Every quality in the list is first true of Christ himself.
And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
Paul uses the past tense. In Baptism “our old self was crucified with him” (Romans 6:6). What happened in the sacrament must now be lived day by day.
If we live by the Spirit, let us also be guided by the Spirit.
Gift and task in one sentence. The Spirit is already our life; now we must let him lead.
ch: The Catechism, following the Latin tradition, counts twelve fruits of the Spirit: charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, generosity, gentleness, faithfulness, modesty, self-control and chastity (CCC 1832). It quotes verses 19–21 to show the variety of sins (CCC 1852), and it quotes verse 25 to teach that the Spirit is the source of our new life and makes it possible for us to bear fruit (CCC 736). Paul's warning that those who do such things “will not inherit the kingdom of God” is serious, but it is a call to conversion, not a closed door. Grave sin can be forgiven, ordinarily through the sacrament of Reconciliation (CCC 1856).

r.h: The true bread from heaven
set: John 6 begins with the feeding of the five thousand by the Sea of Galilee, when “the Passover, the festival of the Jews, was near” (6:4), and with Jesus walking on the sea (6:16–21). The next day the crowd looks for him and finds him on the other side of the lake. Today's reading opens the long discourse on the Bread of Life, which Jesus gives in the synagogue at Capernaum (6:59).

The conversation moves step by step, from the loaves they ate to the bread the Father gives. The crowd thinks of Moses and the manna; Jesus leads them to himself. The discourse goes on: “I am the bread of life” (6:35), and then, “the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh” (6:51).
str: v. 25: “Rabbi, when did you come here?”
vv. 26–27: not the food that perishes, but the food that endures; the Father's seal.
vv. 28–29: the work of God is to believe.
vv. 30–31: “What sign are you going to give us?” The manna.
vv. 32–33: not Moses but the Father gives the true bread, which gives life to the world.
kw: Jesus plays on the word. They ask what works they must do; he answers that “the work of God” is to believe. Faith is God's work in us before it is ours, and from it all good works grow.
A seal marks what is owned and guarantees that it is genuine. The Father has marked the Son as the one who truly gives the food of eternal life.

In John “true” means the real thing to which earlier signs pointed, as with “the true light” (1:9) and “the true vine” (15:1). The manna was a real gift of God; Jesus is the reality to which it pointed.
vv: you are looking for me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.
Jesus is not scornful of hunger; he has just fed them. But he wants them to see what the bread was pointing to.
Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures for eternal life,
Not a command to stop earning our daily bread. Jesus asks what we spend our deepest effort on.
This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.
The answer is short and searching. Believing is not idle; it is the first and greatest work, and the root of every other.
it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is my Father who gives you the true bread from heaven.
The crowd quoted a Scripture about the manna (Psalm 78:24; see Exodus 16:4). Jesus explains it: the giver was God, not Moses, and the Father is giving now, in the present tense.
ch: The Catechism teaches that St John, in place of an account of the institution, reports the words of Jesus in the synagogue at Capernaum that prepare for the Eucharist: Christ calls himself the bread of life, come down from heaven (CCC 1338). It also teaches that believing in Jesus Christ and in the One who sent him for our salvation is necessary for obtaining that salvation (CCC 161). St Augustine, preaching on verse 29, said: “Believe, and you have eaten” (Tractates on John 25.12, in substance). He did not mean that faith takes the place of the Sacrament. He meant that faith is how we first receive Christ, and that it opens the heart to receive him worthily at the altar.

qa: If faith is “the work of God”, do good works not matter?

They matter greatly, and they are done by grace. Jesus calls faith the work of God because it is God's gift first. From a living faith come works of love, and today's Epistle names their fruit: love, joy, peace and the rest. The Church teaches that, moved by the Holy Spirit and by charity, we can merit for ourselves and for others the graces we need, and eternal life itself, always as God's gift (CCC 2010–2011).
Was the manna only a picture, or was it real?

It was a real gift of God to Israel in the desert, and Jesus does not deny it. He says that the Father who gave the manna now gives the true bread. The manna fed bodies for a time; the bread that Christ gives brings eternal life. The figure was true, and it pointed to something greater.
Does Paul mean that those led by the Spirit can ignore the commandments?

No. The Spirit does not abolish God's law; he writes it within. “There is no law against such things” because love, joy and peace already do what the law asked. Paul says elsewhere that the just requirement of the law is fulfilled in those who walk according to the Spirit (Romans 8:4).
rite: With the First Sunday after Pentecost our Church begins the long series of Sundays after Pentecost, the time of the Church's life in the Spirit. Today's readings join the Spirit and the bread. In every Holy Qurbono the priest calls on the Holy Spirit to come upon the bread and wine, and the faithful receive the Body and Blood of Christ. Mar Aprem sang that in the Lord's bread the Spirit is hidden, who cannot be eaten, and in his wine dwells a fire that cannot be drunk (Hymns on Faith 10, in substance). The fruit of the Spirit in Galatians is the harvest this bread is meant to grow in us. The evening Gospel of the sower reminds us that the word sown each Sunday needs good soil.
study: At Gilgal Israel's first act in the land was the Passover. How does our family begin new stages of life, a new home, a new job, a new school year, with God?
Which fruit of the Spirit is most missing in my life just now? Which work of the flesh most often takes its place?
Jesus says the crowd looked for him because they had eaten their fill. Why do I look for him?
How can I prepare to receive the Holy Qurbono with the faith that Jesus calls “the work of God”?

lead: On the Monday of the first week after Pentecost the Epistle shows the Church as God's house, built of living people on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone, “a dwelling place for God”. The Gospel is the sad close of Jesus' public ministry in John: many signs, little faith, and some who believed but were afraid to say so, “for they loved human glory more than the glory that comes from God.” The key words are household and glory.

r.h: No longer strangers: a dwelling place for God
set: Ephesians is above all a letter about the Church. The letter names Paul as its author, and the Church's tradition received it as his; many scholars today think it was written by a disciple of Paul in his name, late in the first century. Either way the Church reads it as inspired Scripture.

Just before today's verses the writer reminds the Gentile believers that they were once “far off”, without hope, and that Christ “has broken down the dividing wall” to make Jew and Gentile one in himself (2:13–14). The Gentiles are joined to the promises God made to Israel, not set in Israel's place. Today's verses draw the conclusion with the picture of a building.
str: v. 19: no longer strangers: citizens and members of God's household.
v. 20: the foundation of apostles and prophets; Christ the cornerstone.
vv. 21–22: the building grows into a holy temple, a dwelling place for God in the Spirit.
kw: Two kinds of outsider: the foreigner passing through, and the resident alien who lived in a place without a citizen's rights. Now the Gentile believers are “citizens with the saints” and members of God's own family.

The stone that holds the building together and fixes its lines. The image comes from Isaiah 28:16, “a precious cornerstone”, and Psalm 118:22, “the stone that the builders rejected”. Some scholars think it may mean the top stone that completes the arch. Either way, the whole building depends on Christ.
vv: So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God,
From outsiders to family. In the Church no one is a guest on sufferance. Every baptized person belongs to the household.
in whom you also are built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God.
The Greek says “in the Spirit”. The temple of stone in Jerusalem was the place of God's presence; now the Spirit makes a people into his dwelling.
ch: The Catechism gathers the Bible's images of the Church as a building: the house of God in which his family dwells, built on the apostles, with Christ as the cornerstone (CCC 756). It teaches that the Church is the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is to the Body of Christ what the soul is to the human body (CCC 797–798). In a parish this means that the living stones matter more than the walls, and that no one should feel a stranger there.

r.h: They loved human glory more than the glory of God
set: These verses close the first half of John's Gospel, often called the Book of Signs (chapters 1–12). Jesus has worked his great signs, the last of them the raising of Lazarus (chapter 11). He has entered Jerusalem and spoken of the grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit (12:24). Now John steps back and asks why so many did not believe, and he answers with two passages of Isaiah.

Jesus, his mother and all the first disciples were Jews. When John speaks of opposition, he usually means the religious authorities in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as such. In today's passage John himself says that many, even of the authorities, believed in him.
str: v. 37: many signs, yet they did not believe.
vv. 38–40: two words of Isaiah (53:1; 6:10).
v. 41: Isaiah saw his glory.
vv. 42–43: believers who would not confess, for fear and for love of human glory.
kw: John's word for Jesus' miracles: deeds that point beyond themselves to who he is. Signs invite faith; they do not force it.

The same word is used in v. 41 of the glory Isaiah saw and in v. 43 of “human glory”, meaning praise or reputation. John sets the two side by side: the glory of God shown in Jesus, and the small glory of what others think of us.

A word found only in John (9:22; 12:42; 16:2). Many scholars think it reflects the painful separation between synagogue and Church later in the first century, as well as tensions already present in Jesus' lifetime.
vv: Although he had performed so many signs in their presence, they did not believe in him.
An honest admission. Even the clearest signs do not compel belief. Faith remains an answer of the heart.
Isaiah said this because he saw his glory and spoke about him.
Isaiah saw the Lord on his throne in the temple (Isaiah 6:1). John says that the glory Isaiah saw was the glory of the Son. The Word was already at work in Israel's history before he became flesh.
for they loved human glory more than the glory that comes from God.
The quiet sin of good people: not hatred of Jesus, but fear of what others will say. John names it so that we may examine ourselves.
ch: The Church does not read Isaiah's words about blinded eyes as God forcing anyone to refuse him. The prophet speaks of the result of a long refusal as if it were God's own act, because nothing happens outside his providence. St Augustine explained that God blinds and hardens not by making anyone evil, but by leaving people to the darkness they have chosen (Tractates on John 53, in substance). The Church also forbids reading this passage as a judgement on the Jewish people: what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). The question John asks is for every reader.

qa: Does verse 39 mean that they could not believe even if they wanted to?

No. The Bible often speaks of God's permission as if it were his direct action. The people John describes had already seen many signs and refused them. Isaiah's words describe how a heart grows hard by refusing light. God “desires everyone to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4), and no one is predestined to refuse him (CCC 1037).
study: Is there anyone in our parish who might feel like a “stranger”? What could I do this week to make them feel part of the household?
Where do I keep silent about my faith because I fear what others will say?

lead: Both readings today are about the time in between: the time after the Lord has gone to the Father and before he returns. Paul tells the Corinthians how to live it when the body grows weak: “we do not lose heart”, because something within is being renewed day by day. In Luke the nobleman goes away to receive royal power and leaves his servants with one pound each and a single command: “Do business with these until I come back.” The key words are renewal and faithfulness.

r.h: We do not lose heart
set: Paul wrote 2 Corinthians from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–57, in a hard season of his ministry. In chapter 4 he speaks of the Gospel as a treasure carried “in clay jars” (4:7), and of himself as “afflicted in every way, but not crushed” (4:8). Just before our verses he gives the ground of his hope: the one who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also (4:14). Today's three verses draw the conclusion.
str: v. 16: we do not lose heart: the outer nature wastes away, the inner nature is renewed.
v. 17: light and passing affliction set beside an eternal weight of glory.
v. 18: what is seen and passes, and what is unseen and lasts.
kw: The same words open the chapter (4:1). To lose heart is to give up in weariness. Paul does not say he never feels tired. He says he does not give in to it.

Literally “the outer person” and “the inner person”. Paul is not dividing body from soul as if the body did not matter. The outer person is our life as it can be seen and as it ages; the inner person is the life that God is making new in us.
In Hebrew the word for glory, kābôd, also carries the sense of weight. Paul puts the two on a scale: the affliction is light, the glory is heavy.
vv: Even though our outer nature is wasting away, our inner nature is being renewed day by day.
“Day by day” is the rhythm of grace. Renewal is not only a single event at Baptism. It goes on in every day that is lived with Christ, even in old age and sickness.
For this slight momentary affliction is preparing us for an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure,

Paul had been beaten, shipwrecked and imprisoned (11:23–27). He calls it “slight” and “momentary” only because he has set it beside eternity. In Romans he says the same: the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed (Romans 8:18).
because we look not at what can be seen but at what cannot be seen;
The verb means to keep one's eyes fixed on a goal, as a runner looks at the finish.
ch: The Church hears in these verses the virtue of hope, by which we desire eternal life as our happiness and rely not on our own strength but on the grace of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1817). They are often read at funerals and in the care of the sick, because they say what faith sees when the body fails. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this letter, says that Paul makes affliction light by setting it beside the reward, and short by setting it beside eternity (Homilies on 2 Corinthians, in substance).

r.h: Do business with these until I come back
set: Jesus is now near Jerusalem. He has just stayed in the house of Zacchaeus at Jericho (19:1–10), and the next scene is his entry into the city (19:28–40). Luke says why he tells this parable: the crowd “supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately” (19:11). The parable answers that there will be a time of absence first, and a time of work.

The story would have sounded familiar. When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus went to Rome to have his kingship confirmed by the emperor, and a delegation followed him to oppose it (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 17). Jesus uses this kind of event as the frame of his story. Matthew has a similar parable with talents (Matthew 25:14–30), but in Luke every servant receives the same sum: one mina, about a hundred days' wages.
str: v. 11: why the parable is told.
vv. 12–14: the nobleman leaves; ten servants receive a pound each; the citizens refuse him.
vv. 15–19: he returns as king; two servants are rewarded with cities.
vv. 20–26: the third servant, who hid the pound out of fear.
v. 27: judgment on those who refused his rule.
kw: A Greek sum of money worth a hundred drachmas. It is not a fortune. The servants are tested on something modest, so that faithfulness, not natural ability, is what counts.
To trade, to put to work. The gift is not given to be kept safe but to be used and to grow.
The master's praise is not “successful” but “trustworthy”. The same word is used of the faithful steward in 12:42 and of being faithful in a very little in 16:10.
vv: Do business with these until I come back.

These words describe the life of the Church between the Ascension and the Lord's return. Luke opens Acts with the same horizon: “This Jesus… will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11).
Well done, good slave! Because you have been trustworthy in a very small thing, take charge of ten cities.
The reward is far beyond the work. A single pound becomes authority over ten cities. God is never outdone in generosity.
for I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man;
The third servant does nothing wrong with the money; he simply does nothing. What paralyses him is a false picture of his master. He is judged “by your own words” (19:22).
I tell you, to all those who have, more will be given;
A law of the spiritual life: grace used grows, grace buried withers.
ch: Many interpreters see in the one pound the gift that every Christian receives alike, such as the word of God and the grace of Baptism, and in the cities the share in Christ's reign that he gives to the faithful. The harsh last verse belongs to the world of the story, where kings punished rebels. It is a warning that to refuse Christ's kingship has consequences, not a picture of a cruel Jesus: in the very next scene he weeps over Jerusalem (19:41). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is a pilgrim, already sharing in the last age, who waits for the Lord's return and works while she waits (Lumen Gentium 48).

qa: Is God really a harsh master who reaps where he did not sow?

No. Those are the frightened servant's words, not the truth about the master, who in fact gives cities for a pound. The parable shows how fear can freeze a believer. St John writes: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). We work for the Lord not as slaves who dread him but as children who trust him.
rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Sophia, without saying which of the holy women of that name is meant. The name itself is a word to pray with: sophia is Greek for wisdom. Today's readings show what that wisdom is: to weigh things by eternity, and to use faithfully, while we wait, what the Lord has entrusted to us.
study: What is the “one pound” the Lord has given me, and am I trading with it or keeping it wrapped in a cloth?
Paul's outer nature was wasting away. Where do I see my own inner nature being renewed day by day, and how can the Holy Qurbono feed that renewal?

lead: Today's readings are about how the word of God is received. Paul thanks God that the Thessalonians accepted his preaching “not as a human word but as what it really is, God's word”, and he knows what it cost them. In the Gospel many disciples have turned away after the teaching on the bread of life, and Peter answers for the Twelve: “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.” The key words are receive and believe.

r.h: Not as a human word but as God's word
set: 1 Thessalonians is very probably the oldest writing in the New Testament, sent by Paul from Corinth around AD 50–51. Acts tells how Paul preached in the synagogue of Thessalonica, how some Jews and many Greeks believed, and how opposition forced him to leave by night (Acts 17:1–10). The young church had suffered from the start.

Verses 14–16 contain the sharpest words Paul ever wrote about some of his own people. They must be read with care. Paul was himself a Jew, proud of his people and grieving for them (Romans 9:1–5; 11:1). Here he speaks of particular opponents in Judea who had persecuted the churches there and tried to stop the preaching to the Gentiles, just as the Thessalonians suffered from “your own compatriots”. A few scholars have thought these verses were added later, but most accept them as Paul's. Either way, the Church reads them in the light of his mature teaching in Romans 9–11.
str: v. 13: thanksgiving: the word received as God's word, at work in believers.
v. 14: the Thessalonians share the sufferings of the churches in Judea.
vv. 15–16: Paul's complaint against those who opposed the Gospel and hindered his mission.
kw: Two verbs. The first is the word for receiving a tradition handed on, used of the Lord's Supper and of the Resurrection (1 Corinthians 11:23; 15:3). The second means to welcome a guest. The Thessalonians did both: they took in the teaching and made it at home in their hearts.
From this verb comes our word “energy”. God's word is not a dead letter. It goes on working in those who believe.
The Thessalonians did not set out to imitate anyone's sufferings. They found themselves walking the same road as the first churches, and so they became, in Paul's eyes, part of one family.
vv: you accepted it not as a human word but as what it really is, God’s word, which is also at work in you believers.
Paul does not deny that he spoke with a human voice. He says that through his human words God himself was speaking. This is how the Church understands all preaching that is faithful to the apostles.
For you, brothers and sisters, became imitators of the churches of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea,
The first Christians in Judea were themselves Jews. Paul's comparison is between persecuted believers in two places, not between two peoples.
by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles so that they may be saved.
This is the heart of Paul's complaint: not who these opponents were, but that they tried to block the Gospel. Scholars do not agree what event Paul means by the “wrath” at the end of the verse.
ch: The Catechism takes up verse 13 to describe how the Church receives Scripture: she welcomes it not as a human word but as what it really is, the word of God, and finds in it her nourishment and her strength (CCC 104). On verses 14–16 the Church is clear. The Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today, and that the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). Paul himself writes later that “God has not rejected his people” (Romans 11:1–2) and that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).

r.h: Lord, to whom can we go?
set: These verses close the long sixth chapter of John. Jesus has fed the five thousand and then, in the synagogue at Capernaum (6:59), has spoken of himself as the bread of life and of eating his flesh and drinking his blood. Many disciples say, “This teaching is difficult” (6:60), and many turn back (6:66). This is the first time John names “the twelve”. John has no scene at Caesarea Philippi; this is his form of Peter's confession.
str: v. 67: Jesus' question to the Twelve.
v. 68: Peter's answer: there is no one else to go to.
v. 69: Peter's confession of faith.
kw: Peter repeats what Jesus has just said: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (6:63). The words that drove others away are the very words Peter cannot leave.
we have come to believe and know
Both verbs are in a tense that speaks of a settled state: we have believed and we still believe; we have come to know and we still know. Faith comes first, and knowledge grows from it.
A rare title. In the other Gospels it is spoken by an unclean spirit (Mark 1:24; Luke 4:34). Here it is spoken by a disciple in faith. Jesus is the one whom the Father has set apart and sent (10:36).
vv: Do you also wish to go away?
Jesus does not soften his teaching to keep the Twelve. He respects their freedom, and the question is a real one.
Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.
Peter does not say that he understands everything. He has looked at every other road and found none that leads to life.
We have come to believe and know that you are the Holy One of God.
Some later manuscripts read “the Christ, the Son of the living God”, the wording of Matthew 16:16. The best manuscripts have the shorter and more unusual title, which the NRSV follows.
ch: The Catechism says that the first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the announcement of the Passion scandalized them, and that the question “Do you also wish to go away?” goes on through the ages, inviting us to discover that only the Lord has the words of eternal life (CCC 1336). St Augustine noted that Peter says “we have come to believe and know”, not the other way round: we believe in order to understand (Tractates on John 27, in substance). That is the faith we bring to the Holy Qurbono: we do not see how the bread becomes his Body, but we believe his word.

qa: Does Paul blame the Jewish people for the death of Jesus?

No. Paul, a Jew himself, complains of particular opponents of his day who persecuted believers and hindered his mission. The Church teaches that the passion of Christ cannot be charged against all Jews of that time or of today, and that all sinners were the authors of his sufferings (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598). Paul's own last word on his people is hope: “all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:26).
rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Philip Neri (1515–1595), a priest of Rome born in Florence. He founded the Congregation of the Oratory, where people met to pray, to hear the word of God explained simply, and to sing. He was known for his joy and his humour, for long hours in the confessional, and for his love of the Holy Eucharist. He shows what Peter's answer looks like in a life: a man who had found the words of eternal life and could not stop sharing them.
study: When a teaching of the Church seems hard to me, do I walk away, or do I say with Peter, “Lord, to whom can we go?”
How do I listen to the readings in the Holy Qurbono: as a human word, or as God's word at work in me?

lead: Paul tells the Colossians that their life “is hidden with Christ in God”. In the Gospel a woman tries to stay hidden in the crowd, touches the fringe of Jesus' clothes, and is healed; but Jesus will not let her slip away unnoticed, because he wants to give her more than a cure. The life hidden in God is not a life hidden from God. The key words are hidden and touch.

r.h: Your life is hidden with Christ in God
set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley in Asia Minor, near Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:13). The letter names Paul as its author, writing from prison. Many scholars think it was written by a disciple in his name, perhaps soon after his death; others hold that Paul wrote it himself. Either way, the Church has always received it as inspired Scripture.

In chapter 2 the letter has said that in Baptism the Colossians were “buried with him” and “raised with him” (2:12). Today's verses are the hinge of the letter: they turn from teaching to daily life. What follows in 3:5–17 is very practical: put away anger and lies, put on compassion, forgive one another.
str: v. 1: you have been raised with Christ, so seek what is above.
v. 2: set your minds there.
v. 3: you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
v. 4: when Christ appears, you will appear with him in glory.
kw: A verb with the prefix “with”. The believer's rising is not a separate event from Christ's; it is a share in his. The same compound verb is used in 2:12.
Not a place in the sky, but the world where Christ now reigns “at the right hand of God”, the words of Psalm 110:1. To seek them is to let Christ's reign shape how we live now.
Hidden as treasure is hidden, kept safe, not lost. The new life is real already, but not yet visible to the world. It will be revealed when Christ appears (v. 4).
vv: So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
The “if” is not a doubt. It means “since”. Paul is reminding the baptized of what has already happened to them.
for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
A Christian's deepest identity cannot be seen on the surface. It is kept in God, where no failure or loss can reach it.
When Christ who is your life is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory.
Some ancient manuscripts read “our life” instead of “your life”; the POC follows that reading. Either way, Christ is not only the giver of life. He is our life.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it speaks of the resurrection of the dead: united with Christ by Baptism, believers already share truly in the heavenly life of the risen Christ, but this life remains “hidden with Christ in God” until it is revealed (CCC 1002–1003). Seeking “the things above” does not mean neglecting the earth. The verses that follow fill everyday life, at home and at work, with the virtues of Christ. The Holy Qurbono itself joins earth to heaven: we lift up our hearts to where Christ is, and he comes down to us.

r.h: Daughter, your faith has made you well
set: Jesus has crossed back over the lake after healing the man among the tombs in the country of the Gerasenes (8:26–39). A crowd is waiting for him. Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, begs him to come to his dying daughter, and on the way the woman's story is set inside his. Mark tells the same two stories in the same way (Mark 5:21–43). Both the girl and the woman's illness are marked by the number twelve.

The Law of Moses counted a woman with a long flow of blood as ritually unclean, and the same applied to what she touched (Leviticus 15:25–27). This concerned worship and the Temple, and the Gospel does not dwell on it. But it may help explain why she came quietly from behind.
str: vv. 40–42a: the crowd; Jairus' plea for his daughter.
vv. 42b–44: the woman touches the fringe and is healed at once.
vv. 45–46: “Who touched me?”; power has gone out.
v. 47: she comes trembling and tells everything.
v. 48: “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.”
¶ The story of Jairus' daughter continues in 8:49–56.
kw: Probably the tassel that the Law told every Israelite man to wear on the corners of his cloak, to remember the commandments (Numbers 15:38–39). Jesus wore it as a faithful Jew. Matthew says that many were healed by touching it (Matthew 14:36).
The same word Luke uses of the Spirit's power (1:35; 24:49). Healing is not magic in the cloth. It is the power of God going out from the person of Jesus.
has made you well, has saved you
The Greek verb means both to heal and to save. The POC renders it “has saved you”. The woman came for a cure of the body and received salvation and peace.
vv: She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his clothes, and immediately her hemorrhage stopped.

Twelve years of failure end in a moment. Verse 43 adds that she had spent all she had on physicians; some important early manuscripts leave out those words, and Luke, whom tradition calls a physician (Colossians 4:14), is gentler with doctors than Mark is (Mark 5:26).
Someone touched me; for I noticed that power had gone out from me.
Many pressed on him; only one touched him in faith. St Augustine put it this way: the crowd presses, faith touches (in substance).
When the woman saw that she could not remain hidden, she came trembling;
Jesus calls her out not to shame her but to complete her healing in front of everyone, so that she is restored to the community.
Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.
In all three Gospels that tell this story, she is the only person Jesus addresses as “daughter”. She came as an outsider and leaves as one of the family.
ch: The Catechism recalls that the sick tried to touch Jesus, “for power came out from him and healed all of them” (Luke 6:19), and teaches that in the sacraments Christ continues to “touch” us in order to heal us (CCC 1504). The woman's faith was humble and bodily: she wanted to touch. That is the logic of the sacraments, where the grace of Christ reaches us through water, oil, bread and wine, and the hands of his priests.

study: Where am I hiding from the Lord, as the woman tried to hide in the crowd, and what would it mean to come forward to him?
Paul says my life is hidden with Christ in God. How does that change the way I see my failures and my successes?

lead: Two pictures of love that holds nothing back. Paul, unable to bear the separation any longer, gives up the company of Timothy and sends him to strengthen the young church of Thessalonica in its trials. In the Temple a poor widow puts in two small coins, “everything she had”, and Jesus calls his disciples to look at her. The key words are strengthen and everything.

r.h: We sent Timothy to strengthen you
set: Paul had been forced to leave Thessalonica after only a short stay (Acts 17:10). He went on to Beroea and then to Athens (Acts 17:10–15). From Athens, worried about the new believers he had left behind in the middle of persecution, he sent Timothy back to them. Our passage tells of that decision; a few verses later Timothy returns with good news of their faith and love (3:6). Acts tells the movements of Paul's companions more briefly, and the two accounts are usually fitted together without difficulty.
str: vv. 1–2: Paul stays alone in Athens and sends Timothy.
vv. 3–4: persecution was to be expected; Paul had warned them.
v. 5: his fear that the tempter had undone his work.
kw: To make firm, to set on a solid base. Jesus gives Peter the same task: “strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Strengthening the faith of others is the work of every apostle and pastor.

Literally pressure, being pressed hard. Paul uses it often for the troubles that come with following Christ. He does not promise the Thessalonians that faith will spare them; he tells them that it is “what we are destined for”.
The name Matthew gives to the devil in the desert (Matthew 4:3). Paul sees in persecution not only human hostility but a spiritual attack on faith.
vv: Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we decided to be left alone in Athens;

A few verses earlier Paul said that being separated from them made him feel “orphaned” (2:17, literally). Now he chooses to be left alone for their sake. He feels the absence of his converts as a parent feels the absence of children (see 2:7, 11).
and we sent Timothy, our brother and co-worker for God in proclaiming the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you for the sake of your faith,
Timothy was still young (1 Timothy 4:12), but Paul calls him “co-worker for God”. Some manuscripts have “servant of God”; the NRSV follows the more daring reading.
so that no one would be shaken by these persecutions.
The Greek verb for “shaken” was used of a dog wagging its tail, and so of being flattered or unsettled. Paul fears not only fear itself but being drawn away gently.
I was afraid that somehow the tempter had tempted you and that our labor had been in vain.
Even the great apostle knew anxiety for his people. Pastoral love includes worry, and it turns worry into action: he sends help.
ch: Paul and Barnabas told the first converts the same thing: “It is through many persecutions that we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22). The Church sees in Paul's sending of Timothy the pattern of all pastoral care: the shepherd does not abandon the flock in danger but sends help and seeks news. Today too there are Christians in many lands who suffer for their faith. We pray for them, that no one be shaken, and for those who wrong them.

r.h: She put in everything she had
set: Jesus is teaching in the Temple in the last days before his passion. Just before this scene he warns against scribes who “devour widows’ houses and for the sake of appearance say long prayers” (12:40). Just after it, he foretells that the Temple itself will be thrown down (13:1–2). The widow stands between those two sayings.

The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, where anyone could go. Later Jewish tradition, written down in the Mishnah, speaks of thirteen trumpet-shaped chests for offerings there. Mark explains the widow's coins for readers who used Roman money, which fits the early tradition that he wrote for the Church in Rome.
str: v. 41: Jesus sits and watches the giving; the rich give much.
v. 42: the widow's two small coins.
vv. 43–44: Jesus calls the disciples and teaches them what he has seen.
kw: two small copper coins, which are worth a penny
The lepton was the smallest coin in use. Two of them made a Roman quadrans, a quarter of the Roman as, itself a small copper coin. In money it was almost nothing.
The rich gave from what they had left over; she gave from what she lacked. Jesus measures a gift not by its size but by what it costs.
all she had to live on
Bios means both life and the means of life. She put in, literally, “her whole life”. A few days later Jesus will give his whole life.
vv: He sat down opposite the treasury, and watched the crowd putting money into the treasury.
Jesus watches how people give. Nothing done for God is unseen by him, however small.
A poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which are worth a penny.
She could have kept one coin. She gave both.
Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the treasury.
“Truly I tell you” marks a solemn teaching. Jesus calls his disciples especially to hear it, for they will be the shepherds of the Church.
but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.

Many commentators also hear a note of sorrow: the system that took her last coin is the same one Jesus has just criticized for devouring widows' houses. The Church's reading has always been above all a praise of her total trust in God.
ch: The Catechism, speaking of poverty of heart, recalls that shortly before his passion Jesus gave his disciples the example of the poor widow of Jerusalem who out of her poverty put in all she had to live on (CCC 2544). She has become the image of every hidden gift: the small offering in the church box, the time given by those who have little time, the prayer of the sick who have nothing else to give. The widow gives two coins; Christ gives himself, and in the Holy Qurbono we offer our small gifts together with his perfect one.

qa: Does this mean that the poor should give away their last money?

No. Jesus does not lay a rule on the poor; he reveals what God sees. The Church also teaches that justice demands care for widows and the poor (James 1:27), and Jesus has just condemned those who exploit them. The lesson is for everyone: God values a gift by the love and trust it carries, and he who gives everything to God is never forgotten by him.
study: Do I give to God from what I have left over, or from what it costs me?
Who in my parish or family needs a “Timothy” sent to strengthen them this week, and could I be that person?

lead: On the eve of the Second Sunday after Pentecost, which our Church keeps as Vocations Day, the readings speak of those whom Christ calls. Paul tells Titus to appoint elders in every town of Crete and describes what a bishop, “God's steward”, must be. In the Gospel Jesus turns to the large crowds following him and tells them plainly what discipleship costs. The key words are steward and cross.

r.h: A bishop, as God's steward
set: The letter to Titus belongs with 1 and 2 Timothy to the Pastoral Letters, written to Paul's co-workers about the life and leadership of the churches. They name Paul as their author. Many scholars think they were written by a disciple of Paul in his name some years after his death; others hold that Paul wrote them near the end of his life. The Church receives them as inspired Scripture whichever view is taken.

Titus was a Greek convert who worked closely with Paul (Galatians 2:1–3; 2 Corinthians 8:23). The letter says Paul left him in Crete to finish organizing the churches there. In these verses the words “elder” (v. 5) and “bishop” (v. 7) seem to describe the same office. By the time of St Ignatius of Antioch, around AD 110, the threefold ministry of one bishop with presbyters and deacons is clearly in place.
str: v. 5: Titus's task: set things in order and appoint elders in every town.
v. 6: the elder's home life: blameless, married once, believing children.
vv. 7–8: the bishop as God's steward: five faults he must not have, six virtues he must have.
v. 9: he must hold firmly to the trustworthy word, to teach and to correct.
kw: The word for a senior member of a community, taken over from the elders of Jewish synagogues. From it come “presbyter” and, in English, “priest”.
Literally one who watches over. The Lord himself is called “the shepherd and guardian (episkopos) of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25). The bishop watches over the flock in his name.
The manager of a household, who runs what belongs to his master and will give an account. The bishop is not the owner of the Church. She belongs to God.
vv: I left you behind in Crete for this reason, so that you should put in order what remained to be done, and should appoint elders in every town, as I directed you:
A young church needs shepherds. Paul does not leave their choice to chance, and he gives authority to Titus to appoint them.
For a bishop, as God’s steward, must be blameless;
Blameless does not mean sinless. It means a man whose life gives no fair ground for accusation, so that the Gospel is not discredited through him.
but he must be hospitable, a lover of goodness, prudent, upright, devout, and self-controlled.
Hospitality comes first. In the early Church travelling Christians depended on it, and the bishop's house was to be open to them.
He must have a firm grasp of the word that is trustworthy in accordance with the teaching,
The shepherd's first strength is not his personality but his fidelity to the apostolic teaching he has received.
ch: The Catechism teaches that, so that the mission entrusted to them might continue after their death, the apostles appointed collaborators and successors, and that the bishops are the successors of the apostles by divine institution (CCC 861–862). On “married only once”, it notes that in the Eastern Churches a different discipline from the Latin Church has been kept for many centuries: bishops are chosen only from among celibates, while married men may be ordained deacons and priests (CCC 1580). Paul's list is also a mirror for every Christian home, where hospitality, self-control and love of goodness are first learned, and where vocations are born.

r.h: Whoever does not carry the cross cannot be my disciple
set: Jesus is on the long journey to Jerusalem that began in 9:51. He has just told the parable of the great dinner, where the invited guests make excuses: a field, oxen, a marriage (14:15–24). Now large crowds are travelling with him, and he turns to tell them what it means to follow. The verses that come next, about building a tower and a king going to war, ask the hearer to count the cost (14:28–33).
str: v. 25: the crowds, and Jesus turning to them.
v. 26: the first condition: to put him above every family bond, and above life itself.
v. 27: the second condition: to carry the cross and follow.
kw: A Semitic way of speaking that means to love less, to put in second place. In Genesis, Jacob “loved Rachel more than Leah” (Genesis 29:30), and the next verse says in Hebrew that Leah was “hated”, which the NRSV renders “unloved” (29:31). Matthew gives the sense: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37).

Luke's word means to carry a load. Every hearer had seen men forced to carry the crossbeam to their execution. Later Luke shows the picture made real in Simon of Cyrene, who carried the cross “behind Jesus” (23:26).
A learner who lives with his teacher. The word appears three times in 14:26–33, each time with “cannot”. Following Jesus is not a matter of being in the crowd.
vv: Now large crowds were traveling with him; and he turned and said to them,
Jesus is not seeking large numbers. He turns to the crowd and invites them to become disciples.
Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and even life itself, cannot be my disciple.
Unlike Matthew (10:37), Luke adds “wife” to the list. The demand is not against the family, which Jesus defends elsewhere (18:20). It sets Christ first, so that even family love is lived in him.
Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.
Not merely suffering, but suffering accepted in following him. The cross is carried on the road behind Jesus, not alone.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ is the centre of all Christian life and that the bond with him takes precedence over all other bonds, familial or social (CCC 1618). It adds that family ties are important but not absolute, and that parents should respect and encourage their children's call to follow Jesus, even in the priesthood or religious life (CCC 2232–2233). That is why Vocations Day is a feast for families: the first “yes” to a vocation is often spoken by a father and a mother.

qa: Does Jesus really want us to hate our parents?

No. The word is a Semitic way of saying “love less” or “put second”, as Matthew's parallel shows (Matthew 10:37). Jesus kept the commandment to honour father and mother and insisted on it (Mark 7:9–13). What he asks is that he be loved first. Those who love him first usually find that they love their families better, not less.
rite: The Panchangam remembers St Theodosia without saying which saint of that name is meant. Her name means “gift of God”, and it fits the eve of Vocations Day: every vocation is a gift of God to the Church, and every priest, religious and catechist was first a gift of God to a family. Tomorrow we pray for those whom the Lord is calling, and for the families and parishes that nurture them.
study: Paul's list of virtues for a bishop is also a list for every home. Which of them does my family most need to grow in?
What “cross” is the Lord asking me to carry behind him this week, and am I carrying it alone or with him?

lead: On the Second Sunday after Pentecost the readings show what the Spirit does with those whom God calls. The evening Gospel (Luke 6:12–23) tells how Jesus spent the night in prayer and then chose the Twelve, and how he proclaimed the Beatitudes: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.” In 2 Samuel 5:1–10 the tribes come to David at Hebron and recall the Lord's word to him: “It is you who shall be shepherd of my people Israel.” In Baruch 1:2–8 the exiles in Babylon weep, fast and pray, and send gifts to Jerusalem. In Daniel 6:25–28, after Daniel has come safely out of the lions' den, King Darius confesses the God of Daniel, “the living God”, whose kingdom shall never be destroyed. In Acts 2:14–21 Peter explains Pentecost with the words of Joel: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.”

We study three readings more closely. Leviticus gives the great command, “You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy”, and shows that holiness reaches from the family table to the altar. Paul tells the Romans that there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus, because the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus now dwells in them. In Matthew, Jesus ends his sending of the Twelve with the cost and the reward of discipleship: whoever loses his life for his sake will find it, and even a cup of cold water given to a disciple will not lose its reward. The key words are holy, Spirit and welcome.

r.h: You shall be holy, for I am holy
set: Scholars call chapters 17–26 of Leviticus the Holiness Code, because of the refrain that runs through them: be holy, for I the Lord am holy. Leviticus took its final form, many scholars think, among the priests of Jerusalem, drawing on older laws. In the book itself these words are given by God to Moses at Sinai, for the whole people.

Chapter 19 is a remarkable mixture. Worship and daily life sit side by side: honour for parents, the sabbath, the ban on idols, the rules for sacrifice, care for the poor at harvest, honest weights, respect for the deaf and the blind, and at its centre the commandment “you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (19:18), which Jesus calls the second great commandment (Mark 12:31). For Leviticus, holiness is not one department of life. It is the whole of it.
str: vv. 1–2: the command to the whole congregation: be holy, because God is holy.
v. 3: reverence for mother and father; keeping the sabbath.
v. 4: no idols, no cast images.
vv. 5–8: the sacrifice of well-being: eaten on the first or second day, burned on the third.
¶ Verses 3 and 4 end with the signature “I am the Lord your God”, and verse 2 with “I the Lord your God am holy”.
kw: The root idea is “set apart”, belonging to God. Only God is holy in himself. Israel becomes holy by belonging to him and living in a way that shows it.
The Hebrew verb is the one used for the fear of God. Respect for parents is almost a religious duty. Unusually, the mother is named first, unlike the commandment in Exodus 20:12.

Also called the peace offering. Part of it was burned on the altar, and the rest was eaten by the worshippers in a sacred meal. It was the sacrifice of communion: God and his people sharing one table.
vv: You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy.
Holiness is not first a moral achievement. It is a share in what God is. St Peter quotes this verse to the Christians of Asia Minor: “be holy yourselves in all your conduct” (1 Peter 1:15–16).
You shall each revere your mother and father, and you shall keep my sabbaths:
The first concrete sign of holiness is the home. The family and the day of rest are where reverence for God is first learned.
When you offer a sacrifice of well-being to the Lord, offer it in such a way that it is acceptable in your behalf.
The worshipper is responsible for how he worships. The gift must be offered in the way God has given, not in a way of our own invention.
It shall be eaten on the same day you offer it, or on the next day; and anything left over until the third day shall be consumed in fire.

The same rule is given in Leviticus 7:16–18. Many commentators think it kept the holy meal close to the offering and stopped sacred food from being treated as common. Verse 7 calls meat eaten on the third day piggûl, something spoiled and unclean.
ch: The Church hears in Leviticus 19:2 the universal call to holiness. The Second Vatican Council teaches that all the faithful, of whatever state or rank, are called to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of charity (Lumen Gentium 40; CCC 2013). Christian readers have also seen in the sacrifice of well-being, offered to God and then shared at a holy meal, a distant sign of the Holy Qurbono, where the one sacrifice of Christ becomes the table of communion. The reverence that Leviticus demands for holy food teaches us how to approach the Body and Blood of the Lord.

r.h: No condemnation for those in Christ Jesus
set: Paul wrote Romans from Corinth around AD 57–58, to a church he had not yet visited. Chapter 7 ends with the cry of a person who knows God's law but cannot keep it: “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” and the answer, “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (7:24–25). Chapter 8 unfolds that answer.

The word “Spirit” occurs about twenty times in chapter 8, more than in any other chapter of Paul. After the great feast of Pentecost, the Church reads this chapter to learn what life in the Spirit means day by day.
str: vv. 1–4: no condemnation: God has done in his Son what the law could not do.
vv. 5–8: two ways of setting the mind: on the flesh, which leads to death, or on the Spirit, which is life and peace.
vv. 9–11: the Spirit dwells in you, and the one who raised Jesus will give life to your mortal bodies.
kw: A legal word: the sentence passed on the guilty, with its penalty. Paul does not say there is no sin. He says the sentence has been lifted for those who are in Christ.
Not the body as such, and not sexuality only. In Paul it means human nature closed in on itself, relying on its own strength apart from God. The body itself is promised resurrection in verse 11.
The direction of the whole person: what we think about, desire and pursue. Life according to the Spirit is a matter of where the mind and heart are turned.
vv: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
“Now” is decisive. Something has changed in history, through the cross and resurrection, and in the believer, through Baptism.
For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free from the law of sin and of death.
The “you” is singular in the best manuscripts; some read “me”. The POC keeps the singular “you”. Paul speaks to each believer personally.
by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and to deal with sin, he condemned sin in the flesh,

“To deal with sin” renders the Greek peri hamartias, the phrase the Greek Old Testament uses for the sin offering in Leviticus. The NRSV notes the other possible rendering, “as a sin offering”. Christ is the true offering that the old sacrifices pointed to.
If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will give life to your mortal bodies also through his Spirit that dwells in you.
