The whole Trinity is in this verse: the Father who raises, the Son who was raised, the Spirit who dwells in us. The hope is not only for the soul but for the body.
ch: The Council of Trent took up verse 1 to teach that in those who are reborn in Baptism God hates nothing, and that there is no condemnation for those truly buried with Christ, even though an inclination to sin, called concupiscence, remains in them for the struggle (Decree on Original Sin, 5; see CCC 1264). The Catechism quotes verse 11 when it teaches the resurrection of the body: God will give life to our mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in us (CCC 989). Pentecost is therefore not only a feast of the past. The same Spirit lives in every baptized person.

r.h: Whoever welcomes you welcomes me
set: Matthew arranges the teaching of Jesus in five great discourses. Chapter 10 is the second, the missionary discourse. Jesus names the Twelve (10:1–4), sends them first to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (10:6), and warns them of persecution, of division even within families, and of the cost of following him (10:16–37). Our verses close the discourse; the next verse says, “Now when Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples…” (11:1).

The passage moves from the cost of discipleship to the reward of those who receive disciples. Behind verse 40 stands a principle well known in Judaism and later written down in the Mishnah: one who is sent is like the one who sends him.
str: v. 38: taking up the cross.
v. 39: finding and losing life.
v. 40: to welcome the disciple is to welcome Christ, and the Father.
vv. 41–42: rewards: for welcoming a prophet, a righteous person, or one of the little ones.
kw: The Greek word can mean life, soul or self. The one who clings to his own life as a possession loses it; the one who spends it for Christ receives it back, now and in eternity.
The word for receiving a guest. It occurs four times in verse 40 alone. The mission of the Twelve depends on homes that open their doors.
Here the disciples themselves, the humble and unimportant messengers of Christ (compare 18:6). The smallest kindness to them is counted as done to him.
vv: and whoever does not take up the cross and follow me is not worthy of me.
This is the first time Matthew's Gospel mentions the cross. The disciples do not yet know how Jesus will die; Matthew's readers do.
Those who find their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.
“For my sake” is the key. Jesus does not ask for loss for its own sake but for love of him. This saying is found in all four Gospels in some form (Mark 8:35; Luke 9:24; John 12:25).
Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.
A chain of sending: the Father sends the Son, the Son sends the apostles. To welcome the messenger is to welcome God himself.
and whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple

Cold water in a hot land is the simplest gift there is. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this verse, points out that it costs nothing, so that no one can excuse himself on grounds of poverty (Homilies on Matthew, in substance).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus is the Father's emissary and that he sends his apostles as the Father sent him, so that whoever receives them receives him (CCC 858). It also teaches that Jesus calls his disciples to take up their cross and follow him, because he wants to associate with his redeeming sacrifice those who are its first beneficiaries (CCC 618). These verses explain why the Church has always honoured those who welcome her missionaries and pastors: the family that houses a priest, the parish that supports a seminarian, the parents who give a son or daughter to God, all share in the reward of the one they welcome.

qa: If there is “no condemnation” for those in Christ, can a baptized Christian still be lost?

Paul's promise is for those who remain “in Christ”. In the same chapter he warns: “if you live according to the flesh, you will die” (8:13). The Church teaches that grave sin freely chosen can destroy charity and the life of grace in the soul (CCC 1861), and that Christ gave the sacrament of Reconciliation for those who fall after Baptism (CCC 1446). Our assurance is hope, not presumption: we trust in God's faithfulness and keep close to him (CCC 2005).
Why does Leviticus put a rule about leftover sacrificial meat next to “You shall be holy”?

Because for Leviticus holiness touches everything: the home, the sabbath, the altar and the table. The rule teaches that what is given to God is not to be handled carelessly. Christians apply the same lesson to the Holy Qurbono, approaching the Holy Mysteries with faith, reverence and a prepared heart.
Does “losing one's life” mean that Christians should look for suffering or death?

No. Jesus asks us to give our lives for his sake, not to seek pain for its own sake. The early Church honoured the martyrs but did not praise those who rushed to give themselves up; the account of St Polycarp's death says so plainly (Martyrdom of Polycarp 4). For most Christians, losing one's life for Christ means the daily gift of self: in a family, in service, in a vocation faithfully lived.
rite: Our Church keeps this Second Sunday after Pentecost as Vocations Day. In the West Syriac tradition the Sundays after Pentecost unfold the life of the Church that the Spirit has gathered, and today's readings fit the day closely: Jesus prays all night before he chooses the Twelve; David is called to be shepherd of God's people; the Spirit is poured out on sons and daughters, young and old; Titus, in yesterday's Epistle, is told to appoint elders in every town. Every vocation, to the priesthood, to religious life, to marriage and to mission, begins with God's call and is carried by the prayer of the Church. Jesus himself told us what to do: “ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:38). Today every family is invited to pray for vocations by name, and to welcome those who answer, as the Gospel says, with at least a cup of cold water.
study: Leviticus says holiness begins with reverence for mother and father and with the sabbath. What would make my home and my Sunday more holy?
Paul says there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. Is there an old guilt I still carry that I need to bring to the sacrament of Reconciliation and then leave behind?
Whom has the Lord sent to me, and how have I welcomed them: priests, religious, catechists, or simply people in need?
On this Vocations Day, whom can I encourage by name to listen to God's call, and how can our family support a vocation in our parish?

lead: Paul gives thanks because the faith of the Thessalonians is growing and their love for one another increasing, even under persecution. In the Gospel Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven at the Last Supper and begins his great prayer: “Father, the hour has come.” He tells us what eternal life is: to know the Father, the only true God, and the one whom he has sent. The key words are growing and knowing.

r.h: Your faith is growing abundantly
set: 2 Thessalonians names Paul, Silvanus and Timothy as its senders. Many scholars think it was written later by a disciple in Paul's name, because its tone and its teaching about the Day of the Lord differ from 1 Thessalonians; others hold that Paul wrote it soon after the first letter, around AD 51. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture.

The church of Thessalonica was still suffering persecution. Some members were also confused about the Lord's coming, thinking that the Day of the Lord had already come (2:2). The letter opens, as Paul's letters usually do, with thanksgiving, and here the thanksgiving is also encouragement.
str: v. 3: thanksgiving for growing faith and increasing love.
v. 4: Paul boasts of their steadfastness among the churches.
vv. 5–7: their sufferings are a sign of God's just judgment; relief will come when the Lord Jesus is revealed.
kw: A rare compound verb, found only here in the New Testament: “grows beyond measure”. Faith is alive. It is meant to grow, like a plant that has taken root.
Not passive endurance but staying power: remaining under a weight without giving way. Paul names it together with faith, as the fruit that persecution has not destroyed.
The Lord's coming is described as an unveiling. Christ is already Lord; at the end his glory, now hidden, will be seen by all.
vv: because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing.
In 1 Thessalonians Paul had prayed that their love would increase (1 Thessalonians 3:12). Now he sees the prayer answered.
Therefore we ourselves boast of you among the churches of God for your steadfastness and faith during all your persecutions and the afflictions that you are enduring.
Paul tells other churches about them. The witness of one suffering community strengthens the whole Church.
This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, and is intended to make you worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering.
Their suffering is not a sign that God has abandoned them. It is a sign that they belong to his kingdom, which the world resists.
and to give relief to the afflicted as well as to us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven
Justice belongs to God, not to us. Paul elsewhere tells believers never to avenge themselves but to leave room for God (Romans 12:19). In the POC, verses 6 and 7 are arranged in a different order.
ch: The Church reads this passage as a word of hope for those who suffer for the faith. The Catechism teaches that on the last day Christ will come in glory to bring about the definitive triumph of good over evil, and that the Last Judgment will reveal that God's justice triumphs over all the injustices committed by his creatures (CCC 681, 1040). We pray for Christians who suffer in many lands, and for those who wrong them, leaving all judgment to the Lord.

r.h: This is eternal life
set: John 17 is the long prayer of Jesus at the end of the Last Supper, just before he goes out to the garden where he will be arrested (18:1). Since the sixteenth century it has often been called the “priestly prayer”, because in it Jesus consecrates himself and offers himself to the Father for his disciples (17:19).

Throughout John's Gospel “the hour” has been coming: at Cana it “has not yet come” (2:4); at the feast his enemies could not arrest him, “because his hour had not yet come” (7:30). In 12:23 Jesus says, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” Now, in prayer, he hands that hour to the Father.
str: v. 1: the hour has come: glorify your Son, that the Son may glorify you.
v. 2: the Son's authority, to give eternal life.
v. 3: what eternal life is.
v. 4: the work finished.
v. 5: the glory he had with the Father before the world existed.
kw: Not sixty minutes, but the decisive time set by the Father: the hour of the cross, the resurrection and the return to the Father, seen as one.
In the Old Testament God's glory is his presence made visible. In John, the glory of Jesus is revealed above all on the cross, where his love goes to the end (13:1).
The verb is in a form that speaks of continuing knowledge. In the Bible to know is not only to have information but to be in a living relationship, as husband and wife know each other.
vv: After Jesus had spoken these words, he looked up to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you,
Jesus prays with his eyes lifted up, as he did at the tomb of Lazarus (11:41). The first word is “Father”, the word on which the whole prayer rests.
And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

Eternal life is not only endless time after death. It begins now, in knowing God. Many commentators think the wording here, with the full name “Jesus Christ”, reflects the evangelist's own confession of faith.
I glorified you on earth by finishing the work that you gave me to do.
On the cross Jesus will say, “It is finished” (19:30). The work is the Father's will, carried out to the end.
So now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had in your presence before the world existed.
The Son existed with the Father before creation, as the prologue says: “In the beginning was the Word” (1:1). The Church confesses this in the Creed: “God from God, Light from Light”.
ch: The Catechism calls this the prayer of the hour of Jesus, rightly named his “priestly” prayer, which takes in the whole economy of creation and salvation, his death and resurrection (CCC 2746–2751). Verse 3 is often quoted in Christian teaching to show that the goal of our life is communion with God. In every Holy Qurbono we are drawn into this prayer, as the priest lifts the gifts and our hearts to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.

qa: Does “the only true God” mean that Jesus is not God?

No. Jesus contrasts the one true God with the false gods of the nations, and in the same breath names himself as the one sent, whom to know is eternal life. Two verses later he speaks of the glory he had with the Father “before the world existed” (17:5). The Church has always read this prayer as the Son speaking to the Father in the unity of the one God (CCC 240–242).
